docs.title: Chapter 10 - StampedLock (High-Performance Locking)
docs.text:
We'll cover:

  • Why StampedLock was introduced
  • Optimistic Reads
  • Pessimistic Reads
  • Write Locks
  • Lock Conversion
  • Internal Working
  • Performance comparison with ReadWriteLock
  • Real-world examples (market data, inventory caches, geospatial services)
  • Interview questions and production pitfalls

StampedLock is considered an advanced concurrency utility and is a favorite topic for Staff Engineer and Architect-level Java interviews because it demonstrates deep knowledge of balancing correctness and performance.

docs.title: Chapter 10 - StampedLock (High-Performance Locking)
docs.text:
"Most applications read data far more frequently than they modify it. StampedLock was designed to make those reads as fast as possible while still maintaining correctness."

Introduced in Java 8, StampedLock is an advanced synchronization mechanism in the java.util.concurrent.locks package. Unlike ReentrantLock and ReadWriteLock, it introduces Optimistic Reading, allowing threads to read shared data without immediately acquiring a traditional lock.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After this chapter, you will understand:

  • Why StampedLock was introduced
  • Optimistic Locking
  • Pessimistic Locking
  • Read Lock
  • Write Lock
  • Lock Conversion
  • Internal Working
  • Performance Benefits
  • Production Use Cases
  • Common Interview Questions

docs.title: 10.1 Why Do We Need StampedLock?
docs.text:
Imagine a stock trading platform.

Every second:

  • 500,000 price lookups
  • 200 portfolio updates
  • 100 administrator changes

The workload is approximately:

Reads  : 99.9%

Writes : 0.1%

Using ReadWriteLock:

Every read still acquires and releases a lock.

This overhead becomes noticeable under extremely high read traffic.

StampedLock reduces that overhead through optimistic reads.

docs.title: 10.2 What is StampedLock?
docs.text:
A StampedLock supports three locking modes:

Write Lock

↓

Read Lock

↓

Optimistic Read

Unlike ReentrantLock, every lock acquisition returns a stamp, which represents the current lock state.

Example:

StampedLock lock = new StampedLock();

docs.title: 10.3 Traditional Read Lock
docs.text:
long stamp = lock.readLock();

try {

    return product;

} finally {

    lock.unlockRead(stamp);

}

This behaves similarly to ReadWriteLock.

Readers can proceed concurrently.

docs.title: 10.4 Write Lock
docs.text:
long stamp = lock.writeLock();

try {

    updateInventory();

} finally {

    lock.unlockWrite(stamp);

}

Only one writer is permitted.

All readers wait until the writer finishes.

docs.title: 10.5 Optimistic Read
docs.text:
This is the most important feature.

long stamp = lock.tryOptimisticRead();

Product p = product;

Notice:

No lock is acquired.

No thread blocks.

The read proceeds optimistically under the assumption that no writer is active.

docs.title: 10.6 Why Is It Called Optimistic?
docs.text:
Because the thread assumes:

"I believe nobody will modify the data while I'm reading it."

If that assumption is correct:

No locking overhead.

Maximum performance.

If not:

Retry using a proper read lock.

docs.title: 10.7 Validation
docs.text:
Every optimistic read must be validated.

long stamp = lock.tryOptimisticRead();

Product p = product;

if (!lock.validate(stamp)) {

    stamp = lock.readLock();

    try {

        p = product;

    } finally {

        lock.unlockRead(stamp);

    }

}

This ensures correctness if a writer modified the data during the optimistic read.

docs.title: 10.8 Internal Working
docs.text:
Execution flow:

Optimistic Read

↓

Writer Modified Data?

↓

NO

↓

Success

------------------

YES

↓

Validation Failed

↓

Acquire Read Lock

↓

Read Again

This fallback mechanism is what makes StampedLock both fast and safe.

docs.title: 10.9 Lock Conversion
docs.text:
One advantage of StampedLock is lock conversion.

Suppose you already hold a read lock.

long stamp = lock.readLock();

Later you decide to update the object.

Instead of releasing the read lock and acquiring a write lock separately:

stamp = lock.tryConvertToWriteLock(stamp);

If successful:

Read Lock

↓

Write Lock

Otherwise, the conversion fails and you must explicitly acquire the write lock.

docs.title: 10.10 Real Example
docs.text:
public void updatePrice() {

    long stamp = lock.readLock();

    try {

        if (priceChanged()) {

            long ws =
                lock.tryConvertToWriteLock(stamp);

            if (ws != 0L) {

                stamp = ws;

                update();

            }

        }

    } finally {

        lock.unlock(stamp);

    }

}

This avoids unnecessary unlock/relock operations.

docs.title: 10.11 Real Production Example
docs.text:
Market Data Cache

public double getPrice() {

    long stamp =
        lock.tryOptimisticRead();

    double p = price;

    if (!lock.validate(stamp)) {

        stamp = lock.readLock();

        try {

            p = price;

        } finally {

            lock.unlockRead(stamp);

        }

    }

    return p;

}

This pattern is common in:

  • Trading systems
  • Analytics engines
  • Pricing services
  • Real-time dashboards

where reads vastly outnumber writes.

docs.title: 10.12 ReadWriteLock vs StampedLock
docs.text: Feature ReadWriteLock StampedLock Multiple Readers ✅ ✅ Exclusive Writer ✅ ✅ Optimistic Read ❌ ✅ Lock Conversion ❌ ✅ Reentrant ✅ ❌ Higher Read Performance Good Excellent (read-heavy workloads)

docs.title: 10.13 Important Limitation
docs.text:
Unlike ReentrantLock:

StampedLock is NOT reentrant.

Example:

writeLock();

↓

call another method

↓

writeLock()

The second acquisition by the same thread will block, potentially causing a deadlock.

This is one of the most common interview questions about StampedLock.

docs.title: 10.14 When Should You Use StampedLock?
docs.text:
Good candidates:

  • In-memory caches
  • Pricing engines
  • Configuration services
  • Routing tables
  • GIS (Geographic Information Systems)
  • Market data feeds
  • Read-heavy microservices

Avoid it for:

  • Write-heavy workloads
  • Recursive locking
  • Complex nested locking scenarios

docs.title: 10.15 Performance
docs.text:
Typical workload:

Reads  = 100,000

Writes = 100

Performance trend:

synchronized

↓

ReadWriteLock

↓

StampedLock (Optimistic Read)

The exact improvement depends on workload characteristics, CPU architecture, JVM version, and contention. Always benchmark with realistic production traffic before choosing a synchronization strategy.

docs.title: Q1. Why was StampedLock introduced?
docs.text: To improve scalability in highly read-intensive applications by introducing optimistic reads and lock conversion.

docs.title: Q2. What is an Optimistic Read?
docs.text: A read performed without immediately acquiring a traditional lock, followed by validation to ensure no writer modified the data.

docs.title: Q3. Why must validate() be called?
docs.text: Because another thread may have updated the shared data while the optimistic read was in progress.

docs.title: Q4. Is StampedLock reentrant?
docs.text:
No.

Unlike synchronized and ReentrantLock, it is not reentrant.

docs.title: Q5. Can StampedLock always replace ReadWriteLock?
docs.text:
No.

It is best suited for read-heavy scenarios and requires more careful programming due to its non-reentrant nature.

docs.title: Production Scenario
docs.text:
Interviewer:

"Your pricing engine performs millions of reads per minute but only a few updates. Which lock would you choose?"

A strong answer:

  • Consider StampedLock with optimistic reads.
  • Validate optimistic reads before using the data.
  • Fall back to a read lock if validation fails.
  • Benchmark against ReadWriteLock because the actual benefit depends on the workload.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
✅ Always validate optimistic reads.

✅ Keep write operations short.

✅ Use lock conversion when appropriate.

✅ Understand that StampedLock is not reentrant.

✅ Benchmark before adopting it in production.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Forgetting to call validate() after an optimistic read.

❌ Assuming optimistic reads are always correct.

❌ Treating StampedLock as reentrant.

❌ Using it in write-heavy applications without measuring performance.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
• StampedLock extends traditional read-write locking with optimistic reads.
  • Optimistic reads avoid locking when no writer is active, improving scalability.
  • Every optimistic read must be validated.
  • StampedLock supports lock conversion but is not reentrant.
  • It is a powerful choice for read-dominant systems such as caches, pricing engines, and market data services.

docs.title: Chapter 11 - HashMap Internals (Source Code to Production)
docs.text:
"HashMap is one of the most frequently used classes in Java, yet one of the least understood. Every senior Java interview eventually reaches the question: 'How does HashMap work internally?'"

This chapter goes far beyond basic usage. We'll explore the internal implementation, performance characteristics, common pitfalls, and why HashMap becomes dangerous in multithreaded applications.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After this chapter, you will understand:

  • Internal structure of HashMap
  • Buckets
  • Hash Function
  • Index Calculation
  • Collision Handling
  • Linked List vs Red-Black Tree
  • Load Factor
  • Capacity
  • Resize (Rehashing)
  • Java 7 vs Java 8
  • Performance Analysis
  • Production Best Practices

docs.title: 11.1 Why HashMap?
docs.text:
Imagine an e-commerce website.

Every request needs to quickly find:

  • Product
  • User
  • Order
  • Configuration
  • Session

Searching sequentially in a list:

User1

↓

User2

↓

User3

↓

User4

Time Complexity

O(n)

With HashMap:

Hash(Key)

↓

Bucket

↓

Value

Time Complexity

Average O(1)

This is why HashMap is one of the most important data structures in backend development.

docs.title: 11.2 Internal Structure
docs.text:
A HashMap is not a giant table of key-value pairs.

Internally, it stores an array of buckets.

Bucket Array

+----+----+----+----+----+----+

0    1    2    3    4    5

+----+----+----+----+----+----+

Each bucket may contain:

  • Nothing
  • One Entry
  • Multiple Entries

docs.title: 11.3 Node Structure
docs.text:
Internally each entry looks like:

static class Node<K,V>{

    final int hash;

    final K key;

    V value;

    Node<K,V> next;

}

Every node stores:

  • Hash
  • Key
  • Value
  • Pointer to next node

docs.title: 11.4 What Happens During put()?
docs.text:
Suppose:

map.put("A",100);

Steps:

Key

↓

hashCode()

↓

Hash()

↓

Bucket Index

↓

Store Node

The key itself is never used to locate the bucket directly; its hash value determines the bucket index.

docs.title: 11.5 Hash Calculation
docs.text:
Example:

"A".hashCode()

Suppose

63215

HashMap further spreads the bits internally before calculating the index to reduce collisions.

Conceptually:

Hash

↓

Spread Bits

↓

Bucket Index

docs.title: 11.6 Bucket Index
docs.text:
Suppose

Capacity

16

Bucket calculation

hash & (capacity - 1)

Example

63215 & 15

↓

Bucket 7

Using a bitwise AND is faster than the modulo operator, which is why HashMap capacities are powers of two.

docs.title: 11.7 Collision
docs.text:
Suppose

"A"

and

"B"

both map to Bucket 7.

Bucket 7

↓

A

↓

B

This is called

Collision.

Collisions are normal and expected.

A good hash function minimizes them but cannot eliminate them entirely.

docs.title: 11.8 Collision Handling
docs.text:
Before Java 8

Bucket

↓

Node

↓

Node

↓

Node

A linked list.

Searching:

O(n)

for that bucket.

docs.title: 11.9 Java 8 Improvement
docs.text:
If a bucket becomes too large,

Linked List

↓

Red-Black Tree

      20

    /    \

   10    30

  /        \

 5         40

Search becomes

O(log n)

instead of

O(n)

This significantly improves performance when many collisions occur.

docs.title: 11.10 Treeification
docs.text:
HashMap converts a linked list into a Red-Black Tree when:

  • Bucket size exceeds 8
  • Table capacity is at least 64

If the table is still small, HashMap prefers resizing instead of treeifying.

docs.title: 11.11 Load Factor
docs.text:
Default:

0.75

Meaning:

Capacity = 16

↓

Threshold

16 × 0.75

↓

12

After inserting the 13th element,

HashMap resizes.

docs.title: 11.12 Resize (Rehashing)
docs.text:
Old Capacity

16

New Capacity

32

Every existing entry is redistributed into the new bucket array based on the new capacity.

Old Table

↓

Recalculate Bucket

↓

Move Node

↓

New Table

Resizing is an expensive operation, so frequent resizing should be avoided by choosing an appropriate initial capacity.

docs.title: 11.13 Why Capacity is Always a Power of Two
docs.text:
Possible capacities:

16

32

64

128

256

Reason:

Fast bucket calculation using

hash & (capacity - 1)

instead of modulo.

This optimization is one of the reasons HashMap is so efficient.

docs.title: 11.14 Time Complexity
docs.text:
Operation Average Worst Case Put O(1) O(n) Get O(1) O(n) (or O(log n) with tree bins in Java 8+) Remove O(1) O(n) (or O(log n) with tree bins)

Average performance is excellent because collisions are usually low when keys have a good hash distribution.

docs.title: 11.15 equals() and hashCode()
docs.text:
One of the most common interview topics.

If two objects are equal,

obj1.equals(obj2)

returns

true

Then

their

hashCode()

must be equal.

Otherwise,

HashMap may fail to retrieve stored values correctly.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
class Employee {

    private int id;

}

If you override

equals()

you should also override

hashCode()

to maintain the general contract.

docs.title: 11.16 Immutable Keys
docs.text:
Good Key

String

Bad Key

class Employee{

    int id;

}

Changing

id

after inserting into the map changes the logical identity of the key.

Retrieval may fail because the object now hashes differently than when it was inserted.

Best Practice: Use immutable objects as keys.

docs.title: 11.17 Real Production Example
docs.text:
Spring Boot Cache

Map<String,User> cache =
        new HashMap<>();

Lookup

cache.get(userId);

Average

O(1)

This makes HashMap ideal for in-memory caches when only one thread is accessing it.

docs.title: Q1. Why is HashMap fast?
docs.text: Because it uses hashing to compute a bucket index, providing average O(1) lookup and insertion.

docs.title: Q2. Why is the capacity always a power of two?
docs.text: To enable efficient bucket calculation using bitwise AND instead of modulo.

docs.title: Q3. What is Load Factor?
docs.text:
The threshold that determines when the HashMap resizes.

Default value:

0.75

docs.title: Q4. Why convert LinkedList into Red-Black Tree?
docs.text: To improve lookup performance from O(n) to O(log n) when a bucket becomes heavily populated.

docs.title: Q5. What happens during resize?
docs.text: A new bucket array is created (typically double the capacity), and existing entries are redistributed into new buckets.

docs.title: Production Scenario
docs.text:
Interviewer:

"Your application stores one million records in a HashMap, but performance suddenly degrades. What would you investigate?"

A strong answer:

  • Check whether the initial capacity was too small, causing repeated resizing.
  • Examine the quality of hashCode() implementations for excessive collisions.
  • Determine whether many entries are ending up in the same bucket.
  • Use profiling tools to identify hotspots.
  • Consider whether another data structure or caching strategy is more appropriate.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
✅ Provide good hashCode() implementations.

✅ Always override equals() and hashCode() together.

✅ Use immutable keys.

✅ Set an appropriate initial capacity when the expected size is known.

✅ Avoid unnecessary resizing.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Using mutable objects as keys.

❌ Overriding equals() without hashCode().

❌ Assuming collisions never occur.

❌ Ignoring initial capacity for large maps.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
• HashMap stores data in an array of buckets.
  • Hash values determine the bucket index.
  • Collisions are handled using linked lists or Red-Black Trees.
  • Java 8 introduced treeification for better worst-case performance.
  • Load factor and capacity directly influence performance.
  • Correct implementations of equals() and hashCode() are essential.

docs.title: Chapter 12 - Why HashMap is NOT Thread Safe (Deep Dive)
docs.text: "This is one of the most frequently asked senior Java interview questions. Many developers know that HashMap is not thread-safe, but very few can explain why."

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After this chapter, you will understand:

  • Why HashMap is not thread-safe
  • Race Conditions
  • Lost Updates
  • Concurrent Resize
  • Java 7 Infinite Loop Bug
  • Memory Corruption
  • Why ConcurrentHashMap was introduced

docs.title: 12.1 The Interview Question
docs.text:
One of the most common interview questions is:

What happens if multiple threads access a HashMap concurrently?

A poor answer:

"HashMap is not thread-safe."

A senior engineer's answer:

"Concurrent modifications can cause race conditions, lost updates, inconsistent reads, structural corruption during resize, and in Java 7 even infinite loops. The appropriate solution depends on the workload, often using ConcurrentHashMap or other synchronization strategies."

docs.title: 12.2 Let's Build a Scenario
docs.text:
Suppose two users transfer money simultaneously.

Both update an in-memory cache.

Map<String,Integer> balances =
    new HashMap<>();

Thread A

balances.put("A",1000);

Thread B

balances.put("B",2000);

Looks harmless.

But internally multiple shared data structures are modified.

docs.title: 12.3 Why is HashMap Unsafe?
docs.text:
HashMap contains shared mutable state.

Bucket Array

↓

Node

↓

next Pointer

↓

size

↓

threshold

All of these fields can be modified during put(), remove(), and resize operations.

There is no internal synchronization protecting these updates.

docs.title: 12.4 Race Condition Example
docs.text:
Initial value

count = 10

Thread A

Read = 10

Thread B

Read = 10

Thread A

Write = 11

Thread B

Write = 11

Expected

12

Actual

11

One update is lost.

The same principle applies inside a HashMap when multiple threads modify it concurrently.

docs.title: 12.5 Concurrent put()
docs.text:
Suppose

Both threads calculate

Bucket = 7

Execution

Thread A

↓

Create Node

↓

Store

--------------------

Thread B

↓

Create Node

↓

Store

Depending on timing:

  • One node may overwrite another.
  • Links between nodes may be broken.
  • Internal state may become inconsistent.

docs.title: 12.6 Structural Modification
docs.text:
HashMap is not just updating values.

It also updates:

Bucket Array

↓

next Pointer

↓

Size

↓

Threshold

Multiple threads changing these simultaneously without coordination can corrupt the internal structure.

docs.title: 12.7 Concurrent Resize
docs.text:
One of the biggest problems.

Current Capacity

16

Threshold

12

Two threads insert the 13th element.

Execution

Thread A

↓

Resize

----------------

Thread B

↓

Resize

Both attempt to redistribute the same nodes.

Without synchronization, the final structure may become inconsistent.

docs.title: 12.8 Java 7 Infinite Loop Bug
docs.text:
One of the most famous concurrency bugs in Java.

During resize,

Thread A

and

Thread B

could reorder linked-list nodes differently.

Example:

Original

A

↓

B

↓

C

Corrupted

A

↓

B

↓

A

A cycle is created.

Searching:

map.get(key);

could loop forever, consuming 100% CPU.

Important: This bug existed in the Java 7 implementation. Java 8 redesigned the resize algorithm and no longer suffers from this specific infinite-loop issue, but concurrent modification of HashMap is still unsupported and unsafe.

docs.title: 12.9 Lost Updates
docs.text:
Suppose

map.put("A",100);

and

map.put("A",200);

run simultaneously.

Final value:

Could be

100

or

200

depending on timing.

Neither thread has any guarantee about which update "wins."

docs.title: 12.10 Inconsistent Reads
docs.text:
Thread A

map.put("A",100);

Thread B

map.get("A");

Without synchronization,

Thread B may observe:

  • Old value
  • New value
  • Intermediate internal state (behavior is undefined under concurrent modification)

This violates thread safety.

docs.title: 12.11 Memory Visibility
docs.text:
Even if Thread A successfully inserts:

map.put("A",100);

another thread is not guaranteed to see the update immediately because there is no happens-before relationship.

Visibility is not guaranteed.

docs.title: 12.12 Collections.synchronizedMap()
docs.text:
Java provides

Map<String,Integer> map =
Collections.synchronizedMap(
    new HashMap<>());

Internally,

every method is synchronized.

put()

↓

Lock

↓

Execute

↓

Unlock

Simple,

but only one thread can access the map at a time.

docs.title: 12.13 ConcurrentHashMap
docs.text:
Designed specifically for concurrent access.

ConcurrentHashMap<String,Integer> map =
    new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

Advantages:

  • Thread-safe
  • High throughput
  • Better scalability
  • No global lock for most operations
  • Supports concurrent reads and many concurrent updates

We'll study its internals in the next chapter.

docs.title: 12.14 synchronizedMap vs ConcurrentHashMap
docs.text: Feature synchronizedMap ConcurrentHashMap Thread Safe ✅ ✅ Entire Map Locked ✅ ❌ Concurrent Reads ❌ ✅ High Throughput ❌ ✅ Scales Well ❌ ✅

docs.title: 12.15 Production Example
docs.text:
Suppose

Spring Boot

@Service
public class SessionCache {

    private final Map<String,Session> sessions =
        new HashMap<>();

}

Thousands of requests:

sessions.put(id,session);

Race conditions become likely.

Correct implementation:

private final ConcurrentHashMap<String,Session>
    sessions = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

docs.title: Q1. Why is HashMap not thread-safe?
docs.text: Because it performs no synchronization while modifying shared internal data structures.

docs.title: Q2. What problems occur?
docs.text:
• Race conditions
  • Lost updates
  • Visibility issues
  • Structural corruption
  • Unsafe resize
  • (Java 7) Infinite loop during resize

docs.title: Q3. Is get() thread-safe?
docs.text: A get() that runs concurrently with writes is not thread-safe. If the map is safely published and never modified afterward, concurrent reads are generally safe.

docs.title: Q4. Does Java 8 fix HashMap thread safety?
docs.text:
No.

Java 8 fixed the specific resize infinite-loop bug from Java 7, but HashMap remains not thread-safe.

docs.title: Q5. Can synchronizedMap replace ConcurrentHashMap?
docs.text: It can provide thread safety, but it serializes access with a single lock. ConcurrentHashMap generally offers much better scalability under concurrent workloads.

docs.title: Production Scenario
docs.text:
Interviewer:

"A Spring Boot service stores user sessions in a shared HashMap. During load testing, sessions disappear and CPU usage spikes. What could be happening?"

A strong answer:

  • Shared HashMap is being modified concurrently.
  • Race conditions may overwrite entries or corrupt internal state.
  • On older JVMs (Java 7), concurrent resize could even create infinite loops.
  • Replace it with ConcurrentHashMap or redesign the shared state.
  • Analyze thread dumps and heap dumps if corruption is suspected.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
✅ Never modify a shared HashMap from multiple threads.

✅ Use ConcurrentHashMap for concurrent access.

✅ Use immutable maps for read-only configuration.

✅ Synchronize external access if HashMap must be shared.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Assuming put() is atomic.

❌ Using HashMap as a shared cache in a web application.

❌ Ignoring resize behavior.

❌ Believing Java 8 made HashMap thread-safe.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
• HashMap is not thread-safe.
  • Concurrent writes can lead to race conditions, lost updates, visibility issues, and structural corruption.
  • Java 7 had a well-known infinite-loop bug during concurrent resize.
  • Java 8 fixed that specific bug but did not make HashMap safe for concurrent modification.
  • For concurrent workloads, ConcurrentHashMap is the preferred choice.

docs.title: Interview Tip
docs.text:
If asked:

"Why is HashMap not thread-safe?"

Don't stop at:

"Because multiple threads can modify it."

Instead explain:

  1. Shared mutable bucket array.
  2. Unsynchronized structural updates.
  3. Resize and rehash issues.
  4. Memory visibility.
  5. Java 7 infinite-loop bug.
  6. Why ConcurrentHashMap solves these problems.

This level of explanation distinguishes a Senior Engineer or Staff Engineer candidate from someone who has only memorized interview answers.

docs.title: 13.1 Why ConcurrentHashMap?
docs.text:
Suppose your application stores:

  • Active Sessions
  • JWT Tokens
  • Product Cache
  • Exchange Rates
  • Configuration

Thousands of users access them simultaneously.

Using

HashMap<String, User> users = new HashMap<>();

creates race conditions.

Using

Collections.synchronizedMap(...)

solves thread safety,

but introduces another problem.

Thread A

↓

LOCK

↓

Thread B waits

↓

Thread C waits

↓

Thread D waits

Only one thread can access the map.

Throughput drops significantly under heavy load.

docs.title: 13.2 Solution
docs.text:
Java introduced

ConcurrentHashMap

to allow:

  • Multiple Readers
  • Multiple Writers (to different buckets)
  • High Throughput
  • Thread Safety

without a single global lock.

docs.title: 13.3 Java 7 Architecture
docs.text:
Before Java 8,

ConcurrentHashMap used

Segments.

ConcurrentHashMap

      |

-------------------------

|     |      |      |

Seg0 Seg1  Seg2  Seg3

Each segment was itself a small hash table protected by its own lock.

docs.title: 13.4 Segment Locking
docs.text:
Suppose

Thread A

writes

Segment 0

Thread B

writes

Segment 3

Execution

Thread A

↓

Segment 0 Locked

-------------------

Thread B

↓

Segment 3 Locked

No blocking.

Different segments could be updated simultaneously.

docs.title: 13.5 Limitation of Segments
docs.text:
Problem:

If two hot keys

belonged to

Segment 2

all writes still blocked each other.

Scalability was limited by the number of segments.

This design was replaced in Java 8.

docs.title: 13.6 Java 8 Architecture
docs.text:
Java 8 removed segments completely.

Now the structure is much simpler.

Bucket Array

↓

Node

↓

Node

↓

TreeNode

Instead of locking an entire segment,

ConcurrentHashMap locks only the bucket being modified.

docs.title: 13.7 Bucket-Level Locking
docs.text:
Suppose

Bucket 2

and

Bucket 9

Execution

Thread A

↓

Bucket 2

------------------

Thread B

↓

Bucket 9

Both execute simultaneously.

This dramatically improves concurrency.

docs.title: 13.8 Lock-Free Reads
docs.text:
One of the biggest improvements.

Example

User user = map.get(id);

No lock.

Reads are generally lock-free and rely on carefully designed memory visibility guarantees.

This allows thousands of concurrent read operations with minimal contention.

docs.title: 13.9 CAS (Compare-And-Swap)
docs.text:
One of the most important interview topics.

Instead of always locking,

ConcurrentHashMap first attempts

CAS.

Conceptually:

Current Value = X

↓

Expected Value = X ?

↓

YES

↓

Update

↓

Done

NO

↓

Retry

CAS is implemented using low-level atomic CPU instructions exposed through JVM primitives.

docs.title: 13.10 Example
docs.text:
Suppose

Bucket empty

Thread A

put("A",100)

Thread B

put("A",200)

Both attempt CAS.

Only one succeeds.

The other retries,

possibly falling back to bucket synchronization if necessary.

docs.title: 13.11 Tree Bins
docs.text:
Just like HashMap,

ConcurrentHashMap converts

Linked List

↓

Red Black Tree

when collisions become excessive.

Benefits:

Search

O(log n)

instead of

O(n)

docs.title: 13.12 Concurrent Resize
docs.text:
One of the smartest engineering features.

HashMap

One Thread

↓

Resize

ConcurrentHashMap

Thread A

↓

Move Buckets

------------------

Thread B

↓

Help Resize

------------------

Thread C

↓

Help Resize

Multiple threads can participate in transferring buckets during resize, reducing pause times under heavy load.

docs.title: 13.13 putIfAbsent()
docs.text:
Instead of

if(map.get(key)==null){

    map.put(key,value);

}

which is not atomic,

use

map.putIfAbsent(key,value);

Entire operation

Check

↓

Insert

is atomic.

docs.title: 13.14 computeIfAbsent()
docs.text:
One of the most useful methods.

User user =
map.computeIfAbsent(

    id,

    this::loadUser

);

Meaning

Exists?

↓

Yes

↓

Return

----------------

No

↓

Create

↓

Insert

↓

Return

The mapping function is applied atomically for a given key.

docs.title: 13.15 merge()
docs.text:
Example

map.merge(

    "A",

    1,

    Integer::sum

);

Useful for counters.

Instead of

count++;

put();

which is unsafe,

merge() performs the update atomically for the specified key.

docs.title: 13.16 Weakly Consistent Iterator
docs.text:
Unlike HashMap,

ConcurrentHashMap

supports iteration

while updates occur.

for(User u : map.values()){

}

The iterator:

  • Does not throw ConcurrentModificationException.
  • Reflects some updates made during iteration, but not necessarily all of them.

This is known as a weakly consistent iterator.

docs.title: 13.17 Real Spring Boot Example
docs.text:
Session Cache

@Service
public class SessionCache {

    private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, Session>
            sessions = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    public void add(Session session){

        sessions.put(session.getId(), session);

    }

    public Session get(String id){

        return sessions.get(id);

    }

}

Thousands of requests

can safely

read and update

the cache concurrently.

docs.title: 13.18 Performance Comparison
docs.text: Collection Thread Safe Read Performance Write Performance HashMap ❌ Excellent (single-threaded) Excellent (single-threaded) synchronizedMap ✅ Poor under contention Poor under contention ConcurrentHashMap ✅ Excellent Excellent for most workloads

docs.title: Q1. Why is ConcurrentHashMap faster?
docs.text: Because it avoids a single global lock by combining lock-free reads, fine-grained synchronization, and atomic operations.

docs.title: Q2. Does ConcurrentHashMap lock the entire map?
docs.text:
No.

In Java 8+, synchronization is generally limited to individual buckets during updates.

docs.title: Q3. Is get() synchronized?
docs.text:
No.

Reads are designed to be lock-free while remaining thread-safe.

docs.title: Q4. Why use computeIfAbsent()?
docs.text: To atomically compute and insert a value only if it is missing, avoiding race conditions.

docs.title: Q5. Can ConcurrentHashMap store null keys?
docs.text:
No.

Neither null keys nor null values are allowed.

This avoids ambiguity in concurrent operations.

docs.title: Production Scenario
docs.text:
Interviewer:

"Your authentication service stores one million active sessions. Thousands of users log in simultaneously. Which map implementation would you choose?"

A strong answer:

  • Use ConcurrentHashMap.
  • Reads remain highly scalable.
  • Updates are synchronized at a fine-grained level.
  • Methods like putIfAbsent() and computeIfAbsent() help avoid race conditions.
  • For distributed deployments, remember that ConcurrentHashMap protects only the current JVM instance.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Using

if(map.get(k)==null){
    map.put(k,v);
}

This check-then-act sequence is not atomic.

Use:

map.putIfAbsent(k,v);

or

map.computeIfAbsent(...)

instead.

❌ Storing null values

map.put("A",null);

Results in

NullPointerException

because ConcurrentHashMap prohibits null keys and values.

❌ Assuming iteration is a snapshot

Iterators are weakly consistent, not immutable snapshots.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
✅ Prefer computeIfAbsent() over manual check-then-put logic.

✅ Use merge() for concurrent counters.

✅ Use immutable value objects whenever possible.

✅ Avoid long-running work inside computeIfAbsent() mapping functions.

✅ Remember that ConcurrentHashMap is thread-safe within a single JVM, not across multiple application instances.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
• ConcurrentHashMap is designed for high-performance concurrent access.
  • Java 7 used segment-based locking; Java 8 moved to bucket-level synchronization.
  • Reads are generally lock-free.
  • CAS reduces lock contention.
  • computeIfAbsent(), putIfAbsent(), and merge() provide atomic operations.
  • Weakly consistent iterators allow safe iteration during concurrent modifications.
  • It is the preferred choice for thread-safe in-memory maps in enterprise Java applications.

docs.title: Chapter 14 - CopyOnWriteArrayList (Thread-Safe List for Read-Heavy Applications)
docs.text:
"What if thousands of threads are reading a list while only a few occasionally modify it? Instead of synchronizing every read, Java takes a completely different approach-it creates a new copy of the list whenever a write occurs."

This is the core idea behind CopyOnWriteArrayList.

It is one of the most elegant concurrent collections in Java and is frequently used in event listeners, observer patterns, Spring Framework internals, and configuration registries.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After completing this chapter, you will understand:

  • Why ArrayList is not thread-safe
  • What Copy-On-Write means
  • Internal Architecture
  • Read Operations
  • Write Operations
  • Snapshot Iterators
  • Memory Trade-offs
  • Performance Analysis
  • Production Use Cases
  • Interview Questions

docs.title: 14.1 Why ArrayList Fails in Concurrent Applications
docs.text:
Suppose multiple threads access an ArrayList.

List<String> users =
    new ArrayList<>();

Thread A

users.add("Alice");

Thread B

users.remove("Bob");

Thread C

for(String user : users){

}

Possible problems:

  • Race Conditions
  • Inconsistent reads
  • ConcurrentModificationException
  • Data corruption

docs.title: 14.2 Traditional Synchronization
docs.text:
One solution is:

List<String> users =
Collections.synchronizedList(
    new ArrayList<>());

Every operation acquires a lock.

Read

↓

LOCK

↓

Read

↓

Unlock

Problem:

Thousands of readers block each other.

Performance decreases.

docs.title: 14.3 The Copy-On-Write Idea
docs.text:
Instead of locking readers,

Java copies the entire array whenever a write occurs.

Original Array

↓

Copy Array

↓

Modify Copy

↓

Replace Reference

Readers continue using the old array.

No blocking.

docs.title: 14.4 Internal Architecture
docs.text:
Internally

CopyOnWriteArrayList

maintains

volatile Object[]

↓

Current Array

Notice

The array reference is volatile.

Whenever a write happens,

a completely new array replaces the old one.

This ensures that readers always see a consistent snapshot.

docs.title: 14.5 Read Operation
docs.text:
Suppose

users.get(5);

Execution

Read Current Array

↓

Return Element

No lock.

No copy.

Extremely fast.

docs.title: 14.6 Write Operation
docs.text:
Suppose

users.add("David");

Execution

Current Array

↓

Copy Entire Array

↓

Add Element

↓

Replace Array Reference

The old array remains unchanged.

Readers continue using it safely.

docs.title: 14.7 Example
docs.text:
CopyOnWriteArrayList<String> users =
    new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();

users.add("Alice");

users.add("Bob");

System.out.println(users);

Every add() creates a new internal array.

docs.title: 14.8 Snapshot Iterator
docs.text:
One of the biggest interview topics.

Example

for(String user : users){

    System.out.println(user);

}

While iteration is happening,

another thread executes

users.add("Charlie");

What happens?

The iterator continues reading

the original snapshot.

It does not see "Charlie" during the current iteration.

docs.title: 14.9 Why No ConcurrentModificationException?
docs.text:
ArrayList

Iterator

↓

Collection Modified

↓

ConcurrentModificationException

CopyOnWriteArrayList

Iterator

↓

Reads Snapshot

↓

No Exception

Because the iterator references an immutable snapshot captured when it was created.

docs.title: 14.10 Internal Example
docs.text:
Initial Array

[A]

[B]

[C]

Thread A starts iteration.

Thread B adds

[D]

New Array

[A]

[B]

[C]

Thread A

continues reading

[B]

The iterator is unaffected by the modification.

docs.title: 14.11 Performance Characteristics
docs.text:
Operation Performance get() O(1) iteration O(n) add() O(n) remove() O(n)

Reads are fast.

Writes are expensive because every modification copies the underlying array.

docs.title: 14.12 Memory Cost
docs.text:
Suppose

Array Size

100,000

One write

creates another

100,000-element array.

Memory usage temporarily doubles until the old array is no longer referenced and becomes eligible for garbage collection.

Therefore,

frequent writes

can create significant memory pressure.

docs.title: 14.13 Real Spring Boot Example
docs.text:
Suppose

Spring maintains

Application Listeners

private final CopyOnWriteArrayList<
    ApplicationListener<?>> listeners =
    new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();

Application events are fired constantly.

Listeners are added

only occasionally.

Perfect use case.

docs.title: 14.14 Event Listener Example
docs.text:
CopyOnWriteArrayList<Runnable> listeners =
    new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();

listeners.add(() ->
    System.out.println("Event"));

for(Runnable listener : listeners){

    listener.run();

}

Multiple threads can safely iterate over listeners while another thread registers a new one.

docs.title: 14.15 Observer Pattern
docs.text:
Used in

  • Notification Systems
  • Plugin Registries
  • Event Publishers
  • Configuration Watchers
  • Monitoring Frameworks

Reason:

Many reads

Few writes

docs.title: 14.16 When NOT to Use It
docs.text:
Avoid

100 Reads

100 Writes

Every write copies the array.

Performance becomes poor.

Better choices:

  • ConcurrentLinkedQueue
  • ConcurrentHashMap
  • Collections.synchronizedList()
  • Other concurrent data structures depending on access patterns

docs.title: 14.17 ArrayList vs CopyOnWriteArrayList
docs.text: Feature ArrayList CopyOnWriteArrayList Thread Safe ❌ ✅ Read Speed Excellent Excellent Write Speed Excellent Slower (copies array) Iterator Fail-fast Snapshot ConcurrentModificationException Yes No

docs.title: Q1. Why is it called Copy-On-Write?
docs.text: Because every write operation creates a new copy of the underlying array before applying the modification.

docs.title: Q2. Why are reads so fast?
docs.text: Readers access the current array directly without locking or copying.

docs.title: Q3. Why doesn't it throw ConcurrentModificationException?
docs.text: Its iterators work on a snapshot of the array rather than the live collection.

docs.title: Q4. Is it suitable for write-heavy applications?
docs.text:
No.

Frequent copying makes writes expensive in terms of CPU and memory.

docs.title: Q5. What is the biggest disadvantage?
docs.text: Every write creates a new array, increasing memory allocation and garbage collection overhead.

docs.title: Production Scenario
docs.text:
Interviewer:

"Your application has thousands of event listeners reading a shared list, but new listeners are registered only a few times each day. Which collection would you choose?"

A strong answer:

  • CopyOnWriteArrayList.
  • Reads are lock-free and highly scalable.
  • Snapshot iterators avoid ConcurrentModificationException.
  • The low write frequency makes the copying overhead acceptable.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
✅ Use for read-mostly workloads.

✅ Keep write frequency low.

✅ Use snapshot iterators when concurrent modification is expected.

✅ Prefer immutable objects inside the list where practical.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Using CopyOnWriteArrayList for write-heavy workloads.

❌ Ignoring the memory overhead of copying large arrays.

❌ Assuming iterators always reflect the latest changes-they reflect the state of the list when the iterator was created.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
• CopyOnWriteArrayList is optimized for read-heavy scenarios.
  • Reads are lock-free and operate on the current array.
  • Every write creates a new copy of the underlying array.
  • Iterators are snapshot-based and never throw ConcurrentModificationException.
  • It is ideal for listener lists, plugin registries, and observer-pattern implementations.

docs.title: Chapter 15 - BlockingQueue (The Producer-Consumer Pattern)
docs.text:
"One of the biggest challenges in concurrent programming is coordinating work between threads. Producers generate tasks, consumers process them. BlockingQueue provides a safe, efficient, and elegant way to connect the two."

BlockingQueue is the backbone of many enterprise systems, including ThreadPoolExecutor, Kafka consumers, asynchronous order processing, logging frameworks, messaging systems, and batch processing pipelines.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After completing this chapter, you will understand:

  • What is a BlockingQueue?
  • Producer-Consumer Pattern
  • Blocking vs Non-Blocking Operations
  • put(), offer(), take(), poll()
  • ArrayBlockingQueue
  • LinkedBlockingQueue
  • PriorityBlockingQueue
  • DelayQueue
  • ThreadPoolExecutor Integration
  • Production Use Cases
  • Interview Questions

docs.title: 15.1 Why Do We Need BlockingQueue?
docs.text:
Imagine an e-commerce application.

Orders arrive continuously.

Customers

↓

Order Queue

↓

Order Processor

If orders arrive faster than they are processed:

  • Orders should wait safely.
  • Consumers should automatically process them when available.
  • Threads should not waste CPU by repeatedly checking for work.

docs.title: 15.2 What is a BlockingQueue?
docs.text:
A BlockingQueue is a thread-safe queue that automatically blocks producers or consumers when necessary.

It provides two key guarantees:

  • If the queue is full, producers wait.
  • If the queue is empty, consumers wait.

This removes the need for manual synchronization using wait() and notify().

docs.title: 15.3 Producer-Consumer Pattern
docs.text:
Producer

↓

BlockingQueue

↓

Consumer

The producer creates tasks.

The queue buffers tasks.

The consumer processes tasks.

Neither side needs to know the speed of the other.

docs.title: 15.4 Creating a BlockingQueue
docs.text:
BlockingQueue<String> queue =
        new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(10);

Capacity

10

Maximum 10 elements.

docs.title: 15.5 Producer Example
docs.text:
queue.put("Order-101");

Execution

Queue Full?

↓

No

↓

Insert

↓

Continue

If the queue is full:

Producer

↓

WAIT

until space becomes available.

docs.title: 15.6 Consumer Example
docs.text:
String order = queue.take();

Execution

Queue Empty?

↓

Yes

↓

WAIT

↓

Item Arrives

↓

Return Item

No busy waiting.

No polling loops.

docs.title: put()
docs.text:
queue.put(order);
  • Waits indefinitely if the queue is full.
  • Guarantees insertion unless interrupted.

docs.title: offer()
docs.text:
queue.offer(order);

Returns

true

or

false

Immediately.

No waiting.

Useful when the application should continue instead of blocking.

docs.title: 15.8 Timed offer()
docs.text:
queue.offer(order,
            5,
            TimeUnit.SECONDS);

Behavior:

Queue Full?

↓

Wait

↓

Space Available?

↓

Yes → Insert

No → Return false

docs.title: take()
docs.text:
queue.take();

Blocks until an item is available.

docs.title: poll()
docs.text:
queue.poll();

Returns

null

if the queue is empty.

docs.title: Timed poll()
docs.text:
queue.poll(10,
           TimeUnit.SECONDS);

Waits for a limited time.

docs.title: 15.10 Complete Example
docs.text:
BlockingQueue<String> queue =
        new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(5);

Thread producer = new Thread(() -> {

    try {

        queue.put("Laptop");

        queue.put("Phone");

    } catch (InterruptedException e) {

        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();

    }

});

Thread consumer = new Thread(() -> {

    try {

        System.out.println(queue.take());

        System.out.println(queue.take());

    } catch (InterruptedException e) {

        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();

    }

});

producer.start();

consumer.start();

Output

Laptop

Phone

docs.title: 15.11 ArrayBlockingQueue
docs.text:
Characteristics:

  • Fixed Capacity
  • FIFO
  • Predictable memory usage
  • Suitable when queue size must be limited

Example:

BlockingQueue<Order> queue =
        new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1000);

Commonly used when back-pressure is important.

docs.title: 15.12 LinkedBlockingQueue
docs.text:
Internally based on linked nodes.

BlockingQueue<Order> queue =
        new LinkedBlockingQueue<>();

Advantages:

  • Optional capacity
  • Higher throughput for many workloads
  • Dynamically grows until the configured limit (or effectively unbounded if no limit is specified)

Suitable for:

  • Thread pools
  • Task scheduling
  • Message processing

docs.title: 15.13 PriorityBlockingQueue
docs.text:
Instead of FIFO,

elements are processed according to priority.

Priority 1

↓

Priority 2

↓

Priority 3

Example:

PriorityBlockingQueue<Task> queue =
        new PriorityBlockingQueue<>();

Used in:

  • Job Schedulers
  • Priority Task Execution
  • Workflow Engines

docs.title: 15.14 DelayQueue
docs.text:
Tasks become available only after a delay.

Example:

Retry Payment

↓

Wait 5 Minutes

↓

Process Again

Used in:

  • Retry Mechanisms
  • Cache Expiration
  • Session Timeout
  • Scheduled Cleanup

docs.title: 15.15 ThreadPoolExecutor Uses BlockingQueue
docs.text:
One of the most important interview topics.

Internally

Client Request

↓

ThreadPoolExecutor

↓

BlockingQueue

↓

Worker Thread

If all worker threads are busy,

incoming tasks wait safely inside the queue.

docs.title: 15.16 Spring Boot Example
docs.text:
@Service
public class OrderProcessor {

    private final BlockingQueue<Order> queue =
            new LinkedBlockingQueue<>();

    public void submit(Order order)
            throws InterruptedException {

        queue.put(order);

    }

    public void process()
            throws InterruptedException {

        while(true){

            Order order = queue.take();

            processOrder(order);

        }

    }

}

This pattern decouples order submission from order processing.

docs.title: 15.17 Kafka Consumer Analogy
docs.text:
Conceptually,

Kafka works similarly.

Producer

↓

Kafka Topic

↓

Consumer

The topic acts as a durable buffer between producers and consumers, much like a queue, although Kafka has different semantics and persistence guarantees than BlockingQueue.

docs.title: 15.18 Performance Comparison
docs.text: Queue Capacity Ordering Best Use Case ArrayBlockingQueue Fixed FIFO Limited queues, back-pressure LinkedBlockingQueue Optional FIFO General task processing PriorityBlockingQueue Dynamic Priority Job scheduling DelayQueue Dynamic Delay-based Retries, expiration

docs.title: Q1. Why use BlockingQueue?
docs.text: It safely coordinates producers and consumers without manual synchronization.

docs.title: Q2. What happens when the queue is full?
docs.text:
• put() blocks.
  • offer() returns false.
  • Timed offer() waits for the specified duration.

docs.title: Q3. What happens when the queue is empty?
docs.text:
• take() blocks.
  • poll() returns null.
  • Timed poll() waits for the specified duration.

docs.title: Q4. Is BlockingQueue thread-safe?
docs.text:
Yes.

Its implementations are designed for concurrent producers and consumers.

docs.title: Q5. Where is BlockingQueue used?
docs.text:
• ThreadPoolExecutor
  • Logging systems
  • Kafka-style processing pipelines
  • Batch processing
  • Asynchronous services

docs.title: Production Scenario
docs.text:
Interviewer:

"Your payment gateway receives 20,000 payment requests per minute, but the payment processor can handle only 5,000 per minute. How would you design the system?"

A strong answer:

  • Place incoming requests into a bounded BlockingQueue.
  • Multiple worker threads consume requests from the queue.
  • A bounded queue provides back-pressure, preventing unbounded memory growth.
  • If the queue fills, decide on an appropriate strategy such as rejecting requests, retrying later, or scaling consumers.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
✅ Prefer bounded queues to avoid uncontrolled memory usage.

✅ Handle InterruptedException correctly by restoring the interrupt status.

✅ Choose the implementation that matches your workload.

✅ Monitor queue depth in production.

✅ Size worker threads based on CPU-bound vs I/O-bound workloads.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Using an unbounded queue without considering memory limits.

❌ Swallowing InterruptedException.

❌ Choosing PriorityBlockingQueue when FIFO ordering is required.

❌ Implementing busy-wait loops instead of using blocking methods.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
• BlockingQueue is a thread-safe queue designed for producer-consumer coordination.
  • Producers block when the queue is full; consumers block when it is empty.
  • Different implementations address different requirements: bounded capacity, priority ordering, or delayed execution.
  • ThreadPoolExecutor relies heavily on BlockingQueue.
  • It is a foundational building block for scalable asynchronous Java applications.

docs.title: Chapter 16 - ConcurrentLinkedQueue (Lock-Free Queue)
docs.text:
"Traditional concurrent collections rely on locks to ensure thread safety. ConcurrentLinkedQueue takes a different approach-it uses lock-free algorithms and atomic CPU instructions to achieve high scalability."

ConcurrentLinkedQueue is widely used in high-throughput messaging systems, asynchronous frameworks, task dispatchers, networking libraries, and low-latency applications.

docs.text:

docs.title: 16.1 Why Another Queue?
docs.text:
Suppose thousands of threads continuously submit tasks.

Using

Queue<Task> queue =
        new LinkedList<>();

Problems:

  • Not thread-safe
  • Race conditions
  • Requires external synchronization

Using

BlockingQueue<Task>

solves thread safety,

but locking introduces contention.

Can we avoid locks entirely?

Yes.

That's exactly why ConcurrentLinkedQueue exists.

docs.title: 16.2 What is ConcurrentLinkedQueue?
docs.text:
ConcurrentLinkedQueue is an unbounded, thread-safe, non-blocking FIFO queue.

ConcurrentLinkedQueue<String> queue =
        new ConcurrentLinkedQueue<>();

Characteristics:

  • Lock-free
  • Thread-safe
  • FIFO ordering
  • High throughput
  • Non-blocking operations

docs.title: 16.3 Internal Structure
docs.text:
Internally the queue is a linked list.

Head

↓

Node

↓

Node

↓

Node

↓

Tail

Each node contains:

class Node<E>{

    volatile E item;

    volatile Node<E> next;

}

Both item and next are updated atomically.

docs.title: 16.4 Lock-Free Algorithm
docs.text:
Unlike

ReentrantLock

↓

Acquire Lock

↓

Modify Queue

↓

Release Lock

ConcurrentLinkedQueue uses

CAS

↓

Success?

↓

YES

Done

↓

NO

Retry

No thread waits for another.

docs.title: 16.5 Michael-Scott Queue
docs.text:
The implementation is based on the famous

Michael-Scott Lock-Free Queue Algorithm

Published in

1996.

Idea:

Tail

↓

CAS

↓

Append Node

↓

Move Tail

Multiple threads may attempt to append simultaneously.

Only one CAS succeeds.

Others retry.

docs.title: 16.6 offer()
docs.text:
queue.offer("Task-101");

Execution

Current Tail

↓

CAS

↓

Insert New Node

↓

Move Tail

No lock.

Multiple producers can insert concurrently.

docs.title: 16.7 poll()
docs.text:
String task =
        queue.poll();

Execution

Head

↓

Read Next

↓

CAS

↓

Move Head

The head advances atomically.

If the queue is empty,

poll() returns

null

It does not block.

docs.title: 16.8 peek()
docs.text:
queue.peek();

Returns

First Element

without removing it.

If empty

null

is returned.

docs.title: 16.9 Producer Example
docs.text:
ConcurrentLinkedQueue<String> queue =
        new ConcurrentLinkedQueue<>();

queue.offer("Laptop");

queue.offer("Phone");

Queue

Laptop

↓

Phone

docs.title: 16.10 Consumer Example
docs.text:
while(true){

    String item = queue.poll();

    if(item != null){

        process(item);

    }

}

Notice

No blocking.

The consumer decides how to behave when the queue is empty.

In many applications, a short backoff strategy or integration with another signaling mechanism is preferable to a tight polling loop.

docs.title: 16.11 Concurrent Producers
docs.text:
Suppose

Thread A

Offer A

Thread B

Offer B

Execution

Thread A

↓

CAS

↓

Success

--------------------

Thread B

↓

Retry

↓

Success

No global lock.

docs.text:
Thread A

Poll

Thread B

Poll

Both attempt CAS.

Only one removes a given node.

Each element is removed at most once.

docs.title: 16.13 ConcurrentLinkedQueue vs BlockingQueue
docs.text: Feature ConcurrentLinkedQueue BlockingQueue Thread Safe ✅ ✅ Lock-Free ✅ Usually No Blocks on Empty ❌ ✅ (take()) Blocks on Full ❌ (Unbounded) Depends on implementation Capacity Unbounded Bounded or Unbounded

docs.title: 16.14 Throughput
docs.text:
Suppose

100 Threads

continuously add tasks.

Performance trend

LinkedList

↓

synchronized Queue

↓

ConcurrentLinkedQueue

Lock-free algorithms generally provide better scalability under high contention, although actual performance depends on workload, hardware, and JVM optimizations.

docs.title: 16.15 Real Spring Boot Example
docs.text:
Task Dispatcher

@Service
public class TaskDispatcher {

    private final ConcurrentLinkedQueue<Task>
            queue =
            new ConcurrentLinkedQueue<>();

    public void submit(Task task){

        queue.offer(task);

    }

    public Task next(){

        return queue.poll();

    }

}

Suitable when consumers periodically poll for work or are triggered by another mechanism.

docs.title: 16.16 Logging Framework Example
docs.text:
Many asynchronous logging frameworks maintain internal queues.

Conceptually

Application Thread

↓

Log Queue

↓

Logger Thread

↓

File

A lock-free queue helps reduce contention when many threads generate log messages simultaneously.

docs.title: Q1. Is ConcurrentLinkedQueue thread-safe?
docs.text:
Yes.

It is designed for concurrent producers and consumers.

docs.title: Q2. Does it use locks?
docs.text:
No.

It uses lock-free algorithms based on CAS.

docs.title: Q3. Does poll() block?
docs.text:
No.

If the queue is empty,

it immediately returns

null

docs.title: Q4. Is it bounded?
docs.text:
No.

It grows as needed until memory becomes a limiting factor.

docs.title: Q5. When should you use ConcurrentLinkedQueue?
docs.text:
When:

  • High throughput is required
  • Blocking behavior is unnecessary
  • Producers and consumers can tolerate polling or have another coordination mechanism

docs.title: Production Scenario
docs.text:
Interviewer:

"You need a high-performance task queue where producers should never block, and consumers periodically check for work. Which queue would you choose?"

A strong answer:

  • ConcurrentLinkedQueue.
  • It is lock-free and highly scalable.
  • offer() and poll() do not block.
  • If consumers must wait efficiently for work instead of polling, a BlockingQueue is a better choice.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
✅ Use when blocking behavior is unnecessary.

✅ Consider backoff strategies instead of aggressive busy polling.

✅ Monitor memory usage because the queue is unbounded.

✅ Design consumers to handle temporary empty queues efficiently.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Using it when consumers should sleep until work arrives.

❌ Assuming it has a fixed capacity.

❌ Forgetting that continuous polling can waste CPU.

❌ Treating it as a replacement for every BlockingQueue.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
• ConcurrentLinkedQueue is a lock-free, thread-safe FIFO queue.
  • It is based on the Michael-Scott algorithm and CAS operations.
  • offer(), poll(), and peek() never block.
  • It is ideal for high-throughput, low-latency systems where producers and consumers do not require blocking coordination.
  • For producer-consumer workflows that require waiting, BlockingQueue is generally the better choice.

docs.title: Chapter 17 - Atomic Classes & Compare-And-Swap (CAS)
docs.text:
The next chapter begins Part IV - Atomic Operations and covers one of the most important foundations of modern concurrent programming:

  • Why synchronized is not always the best solution
  • Hardware atomic instructions
  • Compare-And-Swap (CAS)
  • AtomicInteger
  • AtomicLong
  • AtomicBoolean
  • AtomicReference
  • LongAdder and LongAccumulator
  • ABA Problem
  • CAS retry loops
  • Lock-free programming concepts
  • Production examples (counters, sequence generators, rate limiters)
  • Senior interview questions

This chapter forms the foundation for understanding how high-performance classes like ConcurrentHashMap, ConcurrentLinkedQueue, and many JVM internals achieve thread safety with minimal locking.

docs.title: Chapter 17 - Atomic Classes & Compare-And-Swap (CAS)
docs.text:
"Locks provide correctness by making threads wait. Atomic classes achieve correctness by allowing threads to compete using hardware-supported atomic instructions. Instead of blocking, failed operations simply retry."

Atomic classes are the foundation of many high-performance concurrent data structures in Java, including ConcurrentHashMap, ConcurrentLinkedQueue, ForkJoinPool, and parts of the JVM itself.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After completing this chapter, you will understand:

  • Why Atomic Classes exist
  • Compare-And-Swap (CAS)
  • Hardware Atomic Instructions
  • Lock-Free Programming
  • AtomicInteger
  • AtomicLong
  • AtomicBoolean
  • AtomicReference
  • Atomic Arrays
  • CAS Retry Loops
  • ABA Problem
  • Production Use Cases

docs.title: 17.1 Why Do We Need Atomic Classes?
docs.text:
Suppose multiple threads increment a counter.

count++;

Looks simple.

Internally it performs three operations.

Read

↓

Increment

↓

Write

These three operations are not atomic.

docs.title: 17.2 Race Condition
docs.text:
Initial value

count = 5

Thread A

Read = 5

Thread B

Read = 5

Thread A

Write = 6

Thread B

Write = 6

Expected

7

Actual

6

One update is lost.

docs.title: 17.3 Traditional Solution
docs.text:
Use synchronization.

synchronized void increment() {
    count++;
}

Problem:

Acquire Lock

↓

Increment

↓

Release Lock

Locks introduce:

  • Context switching
  • Waiting
  • Contention
  • Reduced throughput

Can we avoid locks?

Yes.

docs.title: 17.4 What is CAS?
docs.text:
CAS means

Compare-And-Swap

It is a single atomic CPU instruction.

Conceptually:

Current Value = 10

↓

Expected Value = 10 ?

↓

YES

↓

Replace with 11

↓

Success

If another thread already changed the value:

Current = 12

↓

Expected = 10

↓

NO

↓

Retry

No lock.

No waiting.

docs.title: 17.5 CAS Loop
docs.text:
Atomic operations internally use a retry loop.

Read Value

↓

Try CAS

↓

Success?

↓

YES → Done

↓

NO

↓

Read Again

↓

Retry

Only one thread succeeds each time.

docs.title: 17.6 AtomicInteger
docs.text:
Instead of

int count = 0;

use

AtomicInteger count =
    new AtomicInteger();

Increment

count.incrementAndGet();

No explicit synchronization required.

docs.title: 17.7 Example
docs.text:
AtomicInteger visitors =
    new AtomicInteger();

visitors.incrementAndGet();

System.out.println(
    visitors.get());

Output

1

docs.title: 17.8 Common AtomicInteger Methods
docs.text:
incrementAndGet();

Increment then return.

getAndIncrement();

Return current value,

then increment.

decrementAndGet();

Decrease value.

addAndGet(10);

Add a value atomically.

compareAndSet(old,new);

CAS operation.

docs.title: 17.9 compareAndSet()
docs.text:
Example

AtomicInteger balance =
    new AtomicInteger(100);

balance.compareAndSet(
    100,
    200);

Execution

Current = 100

↓

Expected = 100

↓

Update = 200

Returns

true

If another thread changed the balance first:

Returns

false

docs.title: 17.10 AtomicLong
docs.text:
Same concept.

AtomicLong requestCount =
    new AtomicLong();

Suitable for

  • API Counters
  • Metrics
  • Request Tracking

docs.title: 17.11 AtomicBoolean
docs.text:
Example

AtomicBoolean started =
    new AtomicBoolean(false);

Useful for

Application Started?

↓

YES

↓

Skip

Only one thread can successfully change the value from false to true using compareAndSet.

docs.title: 17.12 AtomicReference
docs.text:
Sometimes

objects

must be updated atomically.

AtomicReference<User> user =
    new AtomicReference<>();

Example

user.compareAndSet(
    oldUser,
    newUser);

Useful for immutable object replacement.

docs.title: 17.13 Production Example
docs.text:
Configuration Refresh

AtomicReference<Config> config =
    new AtomicReference<>();

Refresh

config.set(newConfig);

Readers

Config current =
    config.get();

No locking required for replacing the configuration reference.

docs.title: 17.14 Atomic Arrays
docs.text:
Java also provides

AtomicIntegerArray

AtomicLongArray

AtomicReferenceArray

Each element can be updated atomically.

Useful for:

  • Counters
  • Metrics
  • Shared state arrays

docs.title: 17.15 LongAdder
docs.text:
One of the most important interview topics.

Suppose

100 threads

increment

Counter

Using

AtomicInteger

All threads compete for one variable.

Contention increases.

LongAdder works differently.

Cell1

Cell2

Cell3

Cell4

Each thread updates a different internal cell.

Final value

Cell1

+

Cell2

+

Cell3

+

Cell4

Result:

Much higher throughput under heavy contention.

docs.title: 17.16 AtomicInteger vs LongAdder
docs.text:
Feature AtomicInteger LongAdder Single Variable ✅ ❌ (Multiple Cells) Low Contention Excellent Excellent High Contention Good Excellent Memory Usage Lower Higher

Use LongAdder for frequently updated shared counters.

docs.title: 17.17 ABA Problem
docs.text:
Classic CAS problem.

Suppose

Initial

A

Thread A

reads

A

Thread B changes

A

↓

B

↓

A

Thread A performs CAS.

CAS succeeds,

even though the value changed twice.

This is called the ABA Problem.

docs.title: 17.18 Solution to ABA
docs.text:
Java provides

AtomicStampedReference

Each value includes

Value

+

Version Number

Example

A,1

↓

B,2

↓

A,3

CAS detects the version change even though the value returned to A.

docs.title: 17.19 Real Spring Boot Example
docs.text:
API Request Counter

@Service
public class MetricsService {

    private final AtomicLong requests =
        new AtomicLong();

    public void increment() {

    requests.incrementAndGet();

    }

    public long totalRequests() {

    return requests.get();

    }

}

For very high request rates, consider LongAdder instead of AtomicLong.

docs.title: Q1. Why use AtomicInteger instead of synchronized?
docs.text: Atomic classes avoid blocking and generally perform better under low to moderate contention by using CAS instead of locks.

docs.title: Q2. What is CAS?
docs.text:
Compare-And-Swap.

An atomic operation that updates a value only if it still matches the expected value.

docs.title: Q3. Does CAS always succeed?
docs.text:
No.

If another thread updates the value first,

CAS fails,

and the operation retries or handles the failure.

docs.title: Q4. What is the ABA Problem?
docs.text:
A value changes from A → B → A.

A simple CAS cannot detect the intermediate modification.

docs.title: Q5. When should you use LongAdder?
docs.text: For high-contention counters where many threads frequently update the same value.

docs.title: Production Scenario
docs.text:
Interviewer:

"Your API gateway maintains a request counter that is incremented millions of times per minute. Which implementation would you choose?"

A strong answer:

  • AtomicLong is suitable for moderate contention.
  • Under very high contention, prefer LongAdder because it distributes updates across multiple internal cells, reducing contention.
  • If exact intermediate values are needed during updates, evaluate whether AtomicLong better matches the consistency requirements.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
✅ Use atomic classes for simple shared state.

✅ Use LongAdder for high-frequency counters.

✅ Use AtomicReference with immutable objects.

✅ Understand that CAS may retry under contention.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
❌ Replacing every lock with CAS.

❌ Assuming CAS always succeeds on the first attempt.

❌ Ignoring the ABA problem in advanced lock-free algorithms.

❌ Using AtomicInteger for highly contended metrics when LongAdder would scale better.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
• Atomic classes provide lock-free thread safety using CAS.
  • CAS compares the current value with an expected value before updating.
  • AtomicInteger, AtomicLong, AtomicBoolean, and AtomicReference support common atomic operations.
  • LongAdder improves scalability for highly contended counters.
  • The ABA problem can be addressed with versioned references such as AtomicStampedReference.
