docs.title: Are objects stored on the stack?
docs.text:
❌ Generally no.

Objects are typically allocated on the heap. However, modern JVMs may optimise some allocations (for example, through escape analysis and scalar replacement), but this is an implementation optimisation and shouldn't change your conceptual model.

docs.title: Are references stored on the Heap?
docs.text:
❌ Local references are stored in stack frames.

The referenced object lives in the heap.

docs.title: Is Stack shared?
docs.text:
❌ No.

Every thread has its own stack.

docs.title: Can StackOverflowError be fixed by increasing Heap?
docs.text:
❌ No.

Stack and Heap are separate memory areas.

docs.title: Can Metaspace run out of memory?
docs.text:
✅ Yes.

Example:

  • Excessive dynamic class generation
  • Class loader leaks

Error

OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace

docs.title: 18. Production Debugging Story
docs.text:
Problem

Application crashed after several days.

Error

OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace

Investigation

Application repeatedly created new class loaders for dynamically generated classes without releasing them.

Result

Metaspace kept growing.

Fix

  • Eliminate the class loader leak.
  • Reuse class loaders where appropriate.
  • Set monitoring and sensible Metaspace limits.

docs.text:

  2. Difference between Heap and Stack?

  4. Where are local variables stored?
  5. What is Metaspace?

docs.title: 20. Real Interview Scenario
docs.text:
Interviewer:

"Your application throws StackOverflowError. How would you debug it?"

docs.title: Strong Answer
docs.text: I'd first inspect the stack trace to identify repeated method calls, which often indicate infinite recursion. If recursion is intentional, I'd verify that there's a valid termination condition. If the call depth is legitimately very large, I'd consider converting the algorithm to an iterative approach rather than simply increasing the thread stack size.

docs.title: 21. Cheat Sheet
docs.text: Memory Area Purpose Heap Objects and arrays Stack Method frames, local variables, references PC Register Next JVM instruction Native Stack JNI/native methods Metaspace Class metadata

docs.title: Memory Ownership
docs.text: Shared Per Thread Heap Stack Metaspace PC Register Native Stack

docs.title: 🎯 Interview Secret
docs.text:
When the interviewer asks:

"Explain JVM Memory."

Don't just list the memory areas.

A senior-level answer is:

"The JVM separates memory based on responsibility. Shared memory such as the Heap stores application objects and is managed by the garbage collector. Each thread has its own Stack, PC Register, and Native Stack, allowing methods to execute independently without interfering with other threads. Class metadata is stored in Metaspace. Understanding which area is shared versus thread-local helps explain common issues such as OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError, and concurrency behaviour."

That demonstrates both JVM knowledge and the ability to relate it to real production problems.

docs.title: Part VI - JVM Memory Management & Garbage Collection
Chapter 28: Object Creation, Allocation & Escape Analysis (JVM Internals Every Senior Java Developer Should Know)
docs.text:
Interview Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Frequently Asked In: Amazon, Oracle, Microsoft, Goldman Sachs, Visa, Uber, Atlassian

docs.title: 1. Why Do Interviewers Ask This?
docs.text:
This chapter tests whether you understand what actually happens after writing:

new Employee();

The interviewer wants to evaluate your understanding of:

  • Object allocation
  • Heap internals
  • Eden space
  • TLAB (Thread Local Allocation Buffer)
  • Escape Analysis
  • Stack allocation optimizations
  • JIT compiler optimizations
  • Object headers

Typical interview question:

What happens internally when you execute new Employee()?

docs.title: 2. 30-Second Interview Answer
docs.text: When new Employee() is executed, the JVM checks whether the class is loaded, allocates memory for the object (typically in the Eden region of the heap), initializes the object header and fields, invokes the constructor, and returns a reference. Most allocations are fast because they use Thread Local Allocation Buffers (TLABs). The JIT compiler may eliminate some allocations entirely through escape analysis and scalar replacement.

docs.title: 3. Object Creation Lifecycle
docs.text:
Suppose

Employee emp = new Employee();

Internally

Class Loaded?

↓

Memory Allocated

↓

Object Header Created

↓

Fields Initialized

↓

Constructor Invoked

↓

Reference Returned

Every Java object follows this lifecycle.

docs.title: 4. Where is the Object Allocated?
docs.text:
Normally

Heap

↓

Young Generation

↓

Eden Space

New objects are usually allocated in Eden.

docs.title: 5. Memory Layout
docs.text:
Stack

emp

↓

Heap

Eden

↓

Employee Object

The reference lives in the stack frame.

The object lives in the heap.

docs.title: 6. Why Allocation is Fast
docs.text:
Many developers think

new

is expensive.

Usually,

it isn't.

Modern JVMs allocate memory using a simple pointer bump.

Free Memory

↓

Pointer

↓

Allocate Object

↓

Move Pointer

No complex search required.

docs.title: 7. Thread Local Allocation Buffer (TLAB)
docs.text:

docs.title: 10. Escape Analysis
docs.text:
One of the most misunderstood JVM optimizations.

Question

Does every object go to the Heap?

Conceptually, yes.

However,

the JIT compiler may determine that an object never escapes the current method and optimize away the allocation or replace the object with individual fields (scalar replacement).

Example

public int calculate() {

    Point p = new Point(10,20);

    return p.x + p.y;

}

If

Point

never escapes,

the JIT may optimize it heavily.

docs.text:
Suppose

Employee e =
        new Employee();

If

e

is returned

return e;

It escapes.

If

Employee e =
        new Employee();

return e.getSalary();

Object doesn't escape the method.

The JIT has more optimization opportunities.

docs.title: 12. Scalar Replacement
docs.text:
Suppose

Point p =
    new Point(10,20);

Instead of allocating

Point Object

JIT may replace it with

int x = 10

int y = 20

No object allocation.

No GC.

Huge optimization.

docs.title: 13. Stack Allocation?
docs.text:
Interview Trap

Question

Are objects stored on the Stack?

Expected Answer

Conceptually,

Java objects are heap objects.

However,

after escape analysis,

the JVM may optimize allocation so that an actual heap object is unnecessary.

Avoid saying:

"Java stores objects on the stack."

That is an oversimplification and can be misleading.

docs.text:
Interview Favourite.

OOP

means

Ordinary Object Pointer

On a 64-bit JVM,

references are normally 64 bits.

Compressed OOPs store references in a compressed form when possible, reducing memory usage while still allowing access to heap objects.

Benefits

  • Smaller heap footprint
  • Better cache locality
  • Improved performance

Modern JVMs make object creation surprisingly efficient.

docs.title: Is object creation expensive?
docs.text:
❌ Usually no.

Memory allocation is often very fast.

Object initialization and later garbage collection may contribute more to the overall cost.

docs.title: Does every object survive GC?
docs.text:
❌ No.

Most objects die young.

This is the basis of the Generational GC hypothesis.

docs.title: Are immutable objects faster?
docs.text:
Not automatically.

They improve safety and simplify reasoning.

Performance depends on the workload.

docs.title: Does every object reach the Old Generation?
docs.text:
❌ No.

Many objects are reclaimed during young-generation collections.

Application created

Concern

Developers assumed

new

was the bottleneck.

Profiling showed

  • Allocation was inexpensive.
  • Frequent object retention increased GC pressure.

Fix

Reduce unnecessary object retention and reuse expensive resources where appropriate.

Interviewer:

"A developer says new is very expensive and should always be avoided. Do you agree?"

docs.title: Strong Answer
docs.text: Not generally. Modern JVMs allocate most objects using TLABs with a simple pointer bump, making allocation extremely fast. The bigger concern is object lifetime. Short-lived objects are usually collected efficiently, while long-lived or unnecessarily retained objects increase GC pressure. I would profile the application before trying to reduce object creation.

docs.text:
When the interviewer asks:

"Is object creation expensive?"

A senior-level answer is:

"Not on a modern JVM. Most objects are allocated very quickly using TLABs and pointer bump allocation. Instead of focusing on avoiding new, I focus on reducing unnecessary object retention, minimizing GC pressure, and validating performance with profiling tools. The JVM's JIT compiler can even eliminate some allocations through escape analysis and scalar replacement."

This answer demonstrates an understanding of JVM internals, JIT optimizations, and performance engineering, which is exactly what interviewers expect from experienced Java backend developers.

docs.title: Part VI – JVM Memory Management & Garbage Collection
Chapter 29: Garbage Collection Fundamentals & Generational GC (The Foundation of JVM Memory Management)
docs.text:
Interview Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Frequently Asked In: Amazon, Oracle, Microsoft, Goldman Sachs, Visa, Walmart, Adobe, Atlassian

docs.title: 1. Why Do Interviewers Ask This?
docs.text:
Garbage Collection (GC) is one of the most frequently discussed JVM topics in senior Java interviews.

The interviewer wants to evaluate whether you understand:

  • How the JVM reclaims memory
  • Why memory leaks still occur in Java
  • Object lifecycle
  • Young vs Old Generation
  • Minor, Major, and Full GC
  • Object promotion
  • Performance implications

Typical interview question:

Explain how Garbage Collection works in Java.

docs.title: 2. 30-Second Interview Answer
docs.text: Java uses Garbage Collection (GC) to automatically reclaim memory occupied by objects that are no longer reachable. The JVM identifies live objects starting from GC Roots using reachability analysis. Most new objects are allocated in the Young Generation and reclaimed during Minor GC. Objects that survive multiple collections are promoted to the Old Generation, where they are collected less frequently because they are expected to live longer.

docs.title: 3. Why Do We Need Garbage Collection?
docs.text:
Imagine writing:

Employee emp = new Employee();

After the method finishes:

emp = null;

Who frees the memory?

Without GC:

Application

↓

Create Objects

↓

Memory Keeps Growing

↓

Out Of Memory

GC automatically removes unused objects.

docs.title: 4. What is Garbage?
docs.text:
Garbage means:

Objects that are no longer reachable by the application.

Example

Employee e = new Employee();

e = null;

Now

Employee Object

❌ No References

Eligible for garbage collection.

docs.title: 5. Reachability Analysis
docs.text:
Modern JVMs do not simply count references.

Instead, they perform reachability analysis.

GC Roots

↓

Follow References

↓

Reachable Objects

↓

Live Objects

Anything not reachable is eligible for collection.

docs.title: 6. What Are GC Roots?
docs.text:
GC starts from a set of well-known root references.

Common GC Roots include:

  • Local variables in stack frames
  • Active thread references
  • Static fields
  • JNI references

Example

Stack Variable

↓

Employee

↓

Address

↓

City

All remain reachable.

docs.title: 7. Generational Hypothesis
docs.text:
One of the most important JVM concepts.

Observation:

Most objects die young.

Examples

  • DTOs
  • Request objects
  • JSON objects
  • Temporary Strings

Therefore,

the JVM separates memory into generations.

docs.title: 14. Full GC
docs.text:
Interview Favourite.

Full GC generally involves collecting the entire heap and may also reclaim other JVM-managed memory such as class metadata depending on the collector and JVM implementation.

It is usually the most expensive type of collection.

docs.text:
WeakReference<Employee> ref =
        new WeakReference<>(employee);

If only a weak reference remains,

the object is eligible for collection during the next GC.

Typical use:

docs.title: 17. Soft References
docs.text:

        new SoftReference<>(obj);

Softly reachable objects may remain available until the JVM needs memory.

Useful for memory-sensitive caches.

docs.title: 18. Phantom References
docs.text:
Rare interview topic.

Used for:

  • Advanced resource cleanup
  • Tracking object reclamation
  • Integration with ReferenceQueue

Not used to access the object itself.

docs.title: 19. System.gc()
docs.text:
Interview Trap.

System.gc();

Does this force GC?

No.

It is only a request to the JVM.

The JVM is free to ignore it or schedule collection later.

docs.text:

Each request creates

DTO

Response

Validation Objects

Most die within milliseconds.

They are reclaimed during Minor GC.

docs.title: Does GC immediately remove an unreachable object?
docs.text:
❌ No.

The object becomes eligible for collection.

The JVM decides when to reclaim it.

docs.title: Does null immediately free memory?
docs.text:
❌ No.

It only removes one reference.

The object is collected later if it is no longer reachable.

docs.title: Can Java have memory leaks?
docs.text:
✅ Yes.

Example:

static List<Object> cache =
        new ArrayList<>();

If objects remain referenced indefinitely,

GC cannot reclaim them.

docs.title: Does Full GC always mean the application has a memory leak?
docs.text:
❌ No.

Frequent Full GCs may indicate memory pressure, poor tuning, allocation patterns, or a leak. Investigation is required before drawing conclusions.

docs.text:

Logs

↓

Large

HashMap

holding millions of unused objects.

Root Cause

Application cache grew without bounds.

Fix

  • Introduce eviction policies.
  • Limit cache size.
  • Monitor memory usage.

docs.title: 24. Real Interview Scenario
docs.text:
Interviewer:

"Your application throws OutOfMemoryError, but Garbage Collection is running frequently. How is that possible?"

docs.title: Strong Answer
docs.text: Frequent GC doesn't necessarily mean memory can be reclaimed. If objects are still strongly reachable—for example, because of an unbounded cache, a static collection, or a class loader leak—the garbage collector cannot free them. I'd analyse GC logs and inspect a heap dump with tools like Eclipse MAT or VisualVM to identify the dominant retained objects and reference chains.

docs.title: 🎯 Interview Secret
docs.text:
When the interviewer asks:

"Why is Java Garbage Collection efficient?"

A senior-level answer is:

"The JVM is based on the Generational Hypothesis that most objects die young. By focusing frequent collections on the Young Generation, where short-lived objects are created, the JVM avoids repeatedly scanning long-lived objects in the Old Generation. This significantly reduces GC overhead for typical enterprise applications."

That answer demonstrates an understanding of JVM design decisions, not just terminology.

docs.title: Part VI – JVM Memory Management & Garbage Collection
Chapter 30: Modern Garbage Collectors (Serial, Parallel, G1, ZGC & Shenandoah)
docs.text:
Interview Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Frequently Asked In: Amazon, Oracle, Microsoft, Goldman Sachs, Visa, Uber, Atlassian, JVM Performance Interviews

docs.title: 1. Why Do Interviewers Ask This?
docs.text:
Most senior Java interviews eventually include questions like:

  • Which GC are you using?
  • Why G1 instead of Parallel GC?
  • When should you use ZGC?
  • How does Shenandoah differ from G1?
  • How do you choose a garbage collector?

The interviewer wants to know whether you understand real production JVM tuning, not just Java syntax.

Typical interview question:

Which Garbage Collector would you choose for a Java 21 Spring Boot application and why?

docs.title: 2. 30-Second Interview Answer
docs.text: Modern JVMs provide multiple garbage collectors optimized for different workloads. Parallel GC maximizes throughput, G1 GC balances throughput with predictable pause times and is the default in modern JDKs, while ZGC and Shenandoah focus on extremely low pause times for very large heaps. The right choice depends on the application's latency, throughput, heap size, and SLA requirements.

docs.title: Is G1 always the fastest?
docs.text:
❌ No.

It balances throughput and pause times.

docs.title: Does ZGC eliminate all pauses?
docs.text:
❌ No.

It dramatically reduces pause times but still has brief stop-the-world phases.

docs.title: Is Parallel GC obsolete?
docs.text:
❌ No.

It remains an excellent choice for throughput-oriented workloads.

docs.title: Can changing the collector fix a memory leak?
docs.text:
❌ No.

A memory leak is an application problem.

Changing collectors may change symptoms but won't remove the leak.

docs.title: Is CMS still recommended?

docs.text:

docs.title: 23. Real Interview Scenario
docs.text:
Interviewer:

"Your Java 21 microservice has a 64 GB heap. Users complain about occasional multi-second pauses. Which collector would you consider?"

docs.title: Strong Answer
docs.text: I'd first analyse GC logs to confirm that garbage collection is the cause of the pauses. If the application is latency-sensitive and pause times remain unacceptable after tuning G1, I'd evaluate ZGC because it is designed to keep pause times very low on large heaps. I'd also verify allocation rates, object retention, and whether the heap is appropriately sized before changing collectors.

docs.title: 24. Cheat Sheet
docs.text: Collector Best For Serial GC Small applications Parallel GC Maximum throughput CMS Historical (removed) G1 GC General-purpose server applications ZGC Very large heaps & ultra-low latency Shenandoah Very low pause times

docs.title: Selection Guide
docs.text:

docs.title: 🎯 Interview Secret
docs.text:
When an interviewer asks:

"Which GC should we use?"

Avoid giving a one-word answer like:

"Use G1."

A senior-level answer is:

"The choice depends on business requirements. If throughput is the priority, Parallel GC may be appropriate. For most server applications, G1 is a strong default because it balances throughput and pause times. If the application has very large heaps and strict latency SLAs, I'd evaluate ZGC or Shenandoah. Before switching collectors, I'd always analyse GC logs and profile the application because the collector isn't always the root cause of performance problems."

That demonstrates an understanding of trade-offs, performance engineering, and production diagnostics rather than memorising JVM options.

docs.title: 1. Why Do Interviewers Ask This?
docs.text:
This chapter separates developers from production engineers.

Almost every senior Java interview includes a question like:

  • Have you investigated an OutOfMemoryError?
  • How do you analyse a heap dump?
  • Can Java have memory leaks?
  • What tools have you used?
  • What is a ThreadLocal leak?

Typical Interview Question:

Java has Garbage Collection. Why do memory leaks still happen?

docs.title: 2. 30-Second Interview Answer
docs.text: Java can still suffer from memory leaks because the garbage collector only removes unreachable objects. If objects remain strongly referenced—such as through static collections, caches, ThreadLocals, or class loader leaks—the GC considers them live and cannot reclaim their memory. I typically investigate using GC logs, heap dumps, and tools such as Eclipse MAT or VisualVM.

docs.title: 3. Memory Leak vs OutOfMemoryError
docs.text:
Interview Trap.

Many developers think:

Memory Leak

=

OutOfMemoryError

Wrong.

A memory leak

↓

May eventually cause

↓

OutOfMemoryError

But they are different.

docs.title: 4. What is a Memory Leak?
docs.text:
Definition

Memory that is no longer useful but is still reachable.

Example

static List<Employee> employees =
        new ArrayList<>();

Every request

Never removed.

GC sees

Static Reference

↓

Employee Objects

Objects remain alive forever.

Interview favourite.

Store value

Never remove

No

docs.title: 22. Real Interview Scenario
docs.text:
Interviewer:

"A Spring Boot application crashes every three days with OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space. How would you investigate it?"

docs.title: Strong Answer
docs.text: I'd first confirm the error type and review GC logs to understand allocation behaviour. If heap dumps are enabled, I'd open the dump in Eclipse MAT, inspect the Leak Suspects report, review the Dominator Tree and Histogram, and identify the objects with the largest retained heap. Then I'd follow the reference chain back to the GC Root to determine why those objects are still strongly reachable. Finally, I'd fix the underlying cause—for example, an unbounded cache, static collection, or ThreadLocal leak—and validate the fix under load.

docs.title: 🎯 Interview Secret
docs.text:
When an interviewer asks:

"How do you investigate an OutOfMemoryError?"

Don't answer:

"I increase the heap."

A senior-level answer is:

"Increasing the heap may only delay the problem. I'd first determine the type of OutOfMemoryError, analyse GC logs, capture a heap dump, inspect it using Eclipse MAT, identify the largest retained objects and their reference chains, and then fix the underlying cause. Only after understanding the application's memory behaviour would I consider tuning heap sizes."

This demonstrates systematic production troubleshooting, which is exactly what senior interviewers look for.

docs.title: Part VI – JVM Memory Management & Garbage Collection
Chapter 32: JVM Performance Tuning & GC Tuning (Production Performance Engineering)
docs.text:
Interview Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Frequently Asked In: Amazon, Oracle, Microsoft, Goldman Sachs, Visa, Atlassian, Uber, JVM Performance Interviews

docs.title: 1. Why Do Interviewers Ask This?
docs.text:
Most senior Java developers know GC concepts.

Senior engineers know how to diagnose and tune JVM performance in production.

Interviewers typically ask:

  • How do you tune JVM performance?
  • What JVM flags have you used?
  • How do you analyse GC logs?
  • Which JVM tools do you use?
  • How do you investigate high CPU or memory usage?

This chapter focuses on real-world production troubleshooting, not memorising JVM options.

docs.title: 2. 30-Second Interview Answer
docs.text: JVM tuning starts with measuring, not guessing. I first identify whether the bottleneck is CPU, memory, GC, threads, or I/O. I analyse GC logs, thread dumps, heap dumps, and JFR recordings before changing JVM parameters. Heap size, garbage collector selection, and GC tuning should be based on application behaviour and performance goals rather than fixed recommendations.

docs.title: 3. JVM Performance Tuning Workflow
docs.text:
Never start with changing JVM flags.

Follow this workflow:

Performance Problem

↓

Identify Symptoms

↓

Collect Metrics

↓

Analyse

↓

Find Root Cause

↓

Tune

↓

Measure Again

Performance tuning is an iterative process.

docs.title: 4. Common Performance Symptoms
docs.text: Symptom Possible Cause High CPU Infinite loop, excessive computation, GC High Memory Memory leak, oversized cache Long Response Time Slow database, blocking I/O, Full GC Frequent GC High allocation rate, small heap Application Freeze Full GC, deadlock, native issue OutOfMemoryError Leak, insufficient heap, excessive retention

docs.title: 5. Heap Sizing
docs.text:
Most common JVM options:

-Xms2g
-Xmx2g

Where:

  • -Xms = Initial heap size
  • -Xmx = Maximum heap size

Example:

-Xms4g
-Xmx4g

This avoids heap resizing during runtime.

docs.title: 6. Should Xms Equal Xmx?
docs.text:
Interview Favourite.

Production recommendation:

For stable server applications,

-Xms = Xmx

Benefits:

  • Avoids heap expansion pauses
  • More predictable performance
  • Easier GC tuning

For development environments, smaller initial heaps are often acceptable.

docs.title: 7. GC Logging
docs.text:
Never tune GC blindly.

Enable logging.

Java 9+

-Xlog:gc*

More detailed example:

-Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log

GC logs reveal:

  • Pause times
  • Collection frequency
  • Heap occupancy
  • Promotion rates

docs.title: 8. Reading GC Logs
docs.text:
Example

Pause Young (G1 Evacuation Pause)

28 ms

Interpretation:

  • Minor GC
  • Healthy pause
  • Normal behaviour

Another example

Full GC

15.6 s

Investigation required.

Possible causes:

  • Memory leak
  • Heap too small
  • Poor allocation behaviour

docs.title: 9. G1 GC Tuning
docs.text:
Common parameter

-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200

Meaning:

Target

200 ms

Important:

This is a pause-time goal, not a guarantee.

Another useful parameter

-XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent=45

Controls when concurrent marking begins.

Lower values may start marking earlier, depending on workload.

docs.title: 10. ZGC Tuning
docs.text:
Usually requires fewer tuning parameters than older collectors.

Typical configuration:

-XX:+UseZGC

Large heaps often require little additional tuning beyond appropriate heap sizing.

docs.title: 11. Thread Dumps
docs.text:
Interview Favourite.

jstack <pid>

Contains

  • Thread states
  • Stack traces
  • Locks
  • Deadlocks

Useful for investigating:

  • Hanging applications
  • Deadlocks
  • High CPU

docs.title: 12. jstat
docs.text:
Useful command

jstat -gc <pid>

Shows:

  • Heap usage
  • Eden usage
  • Survivor usage
  • Old Generation usage
  • GC count

Good for observing live GC activity.

docs.title: 13. jmap
docs.text:
Generate heap dump

jmap -dump:live,file=heap.hprof <pid>

Analyse later using:

  • Eclipse MAT
  • VisualVM

docs.title: 14. jcmd
docs.text:
Modern JVM diagnostic tool.

Example

jcmd <pid> VM.flags

Other useful commands:

jcmd <pid> GC.heap_info

jcmd <pid> Thread.print

jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram

jcmd is generally preferred over several older standalone tools because it provides many JVM diagnostic capabilities from a single command.

docs.title: 15. Java Flight Recorder (JFR)
docs.text:
One of the best production profiling tools.

Records:

  • CPU usage
  • GC
  • Allocation
  • Lock contention
  • Thread activity
  • I/O
  • Exceptions

Very low runtime overhead.

docs.title: 16. Java Mission Control (JMC)
docs.text:
GUI for analysing

  • JFR recordings
  • CPU hotspots
  • Allocation profiles
  • GC activity
  • Thread behaviour

Frequently used alongside JFR.

I'd review GC logs for long pauses, capture thread dumps if the application appears blocked, and use JFR to collect runtime data if the issue persists. When an interviewer asks:

"I don't begin by tuning JVM parameters. I first determine whether the bottleneck is CPU, memory, garbage collection, threads, or I/O using metrics and diagnostic tools. I analyse GC logs, thread dumps, heap dumps, and JFR recordings to identify the root cause. Only then do I adjust heap sizing, GC configuration, or application code, and I always validate the impact with performance measurements."

docs.title: Part VII – Class Loading, Reflection & Dynamic Proxies
Chapter 33: JVM Class Loading Lifecycle & ClassLoader Architecture
docs.text:
Interview Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Frequently Asked In: Amazon, Oracle, Microsoft, Goldman Sachs, Visa, VMware, Spring Framework Interviews

docs.title: 1. Why Do Interviewers Ask This?
docs.text:
Almost every Java framework relies on class loading.

Examples:

  • Spring Boot
  • Hibernate
  • Tomcat
  • Kafka
  • JUnit
  • JDBC Drivers
  • Logging frameworks

Understanding ClassLoaders helps explain:

  • How Java loads classes
  • Why ClassNotFoundException occurs
  • Why NoClassDefFoundError occurs
  • Hot deployment
  • Plugin systems
  • Memory leaks
  • Spring Boot internals

Typical interview question:

Explain the Java Class Loading process.

docs.title: 2. 30-Second Interview Answer
docs.text: The JVM loads classes on demand using ClassLoaders. The lifecycle consists of Loading, Linking, and Initialization. During Linking, the JVM verifies bytecode, prepares static fields, and resolves symbolic references. During Initialization, static initializers and static variable assignments are executed. Java follows the Parent Delegation Model, where a ClassLoader first delegates to its parent before attempting to load the class itself.

docs.title: 3. Class Loading Lifecycle
docs.text:
Whenever Java executes

new Employee();

The JVM first checks:

Employee.class

Already Loaded?

↓

YES

↓

Create Object

---------------

NO

↓

Load Class

A class is loaded only once per ClassLoader.

docs.title: 4. Complete Lifecycle
docs.text:
Employee.class

                 │

                 ▼

          Loading

                 │

                 ▼

          Linking

     ┌─────────┬──────────┬──────────┐
     ▼         ▼          ▼
 Verification Preparation Resolution

                 │

                 ▼

        Initialization

                 │

                 ▼

        Ready For Use

Interviewers love this diagram.

docs.title: 5. Phase 1 – Loading
docs.text:
Loading means

The JVM finds

Employee.class

and creates

java.lang.Class<Employee>

The bytecode may come from:

  • File system
  • JAR
  • Network
  • Database
  • Custom ClassLoader

docs.title: 6. Phase 2 – Linking
docs.text: Linking has three stages.

docs.title: A. Verification
docs.text:
The JVM verifies that the bytecode is valid.

Checks include:

  • Correct bytecode format
  • Stack usage
  • Type safety
  • Illegal instructions

This helps prevent corrupted or malicious bytecode from executing.

docs.title: B. Preparation
docs.text:
Memory is allocated for static fields.

Example

class Employee {

    static int count = 100;

}

During Preparation

count

↓

0

Only default values are assigned.

docs.title: C. Resolution
docs.text:
Symbolic references are converted into direct references.

Example

Employee emp;

The JVM resolves

Employee

to the actual loaded class.

docs.title: 7. Phase 3 – Initialization
docs.text:
Now static initialization executes.

Example

class Employee {

    static int count = 100;

}

During Initialization

count

↓

100

Static blocks also execute.

Example

static {

    System.out.println("Loaded");

}

Runs exactly once per ClassLoader.

docs.title: 8. Example Timeline
docs.text:
public class Employee {

    static {

        System.out.println("Static Block");

    }

}

Execution

new Employee();

Timeline

Load Class

↓

Verify

↓

Prepare

↓

Resolve

↓

Run Static Block

↓

Constructor

↓

Object Created

docs.title: 9. When Does Class Initialization Happen?
docs.text:
Initialization occurs when a class is actively used.

Examples

new Employee();

Employee.getCount();

Class.forName("Employee");

Simply referring to a class type (for example, declaring a variable) does not necessarily initialize it.

docs.title: 10. ClassLoader Hierarchy
docs.text:
The JVM has a hierarchy of ClassLoaders.

        Bootstrap ClassLoader
                 │
                 ▼
       Platform ClassLoader
                 │
                 ▼
      Application ClassLoader

Each has a specific responsibility.

docs.title: 11. Bootstrap ClassLoader
docs.text:
Loads core Java classes.

Examples

java.lang.String

java.lang.Object

java.util.List

Implemented by the JVM itself.

docs.title: 12. Platform ClassLoader
docs.text:
Loads standard platform modules.

Examples

java.sql

java.xml

java.management

Introduced with the Java Platform Module System.

docs.title: 13. Application ClassLoader
docs.text:
Loads

Your application classes

target/classes

target/test-classes

Application JARs

Most business classes are loaded here.

docs.title: 14. Parent Delegation Model
docs.text:
One of the most common interview questions.

Suppose

new Employee();

Application ClassLoader

↓

Asks Parent

↓

Platform ClassLoader

↓

Asks Parent

↓

Bootstrap

If found

↓

Return Class

Else

↓

Child loads it.

docs.title: Diagram
docs.text:
Application

↓

Platform

↓

Bootstrap

↓

Found?

↓

Yes → Return

↓

No

↓

Child Loads

docs.title: 15. Why Parent Delegation?
docs.text:
Security.

Imagine someone writes

java.lang.String

inside their project.

Without delegation

Application ClassLoader

↓

Loads Fake String

Disaster.

With delegation

Bootstrap already loads the real

java.lang.String

Your fake version is ignored.

docs.title: 16. Class.forName()
docs.text:
Interview favourite.

Class.forName("com.example.Employee");

Loads the class and, by default, initializes it.

Common uses:

  • JDBC drivers (historically)
  • Reflection
  • Plugin loading

docs.title: 17. ClassNotFoundException vs NoClassDefFoundError
docs.text: Very common interview question.

docs.title: ClassNotFoundException
docs.text:
Occurs when the JVM is explicitly asked to load a class (for example, via Class.forName()), but it cannot be found.

Example

Class.forName("abc.Employee");

Result

ClassNotFoundException

docs.title: NoClassDefFoundError
docs.text:
The class was available during compilation, but the JVM cannot use it at runtime.

Possible causes:

  • Missing dependency
  • Failed static initialization
  • Deployment issues

docs.title: 18. Production Example
docs.text:
Spring Boot Startup

Main Class

↓

Application ClassLoader

↓

Spring Classes

↓

Hibernate

↓

Jackson

↓

Tomcat

↓

Application Ready

Thousands of classes are loaded before the application starts serving requests.

docs.title: Is a class loaded every time we create an object?
docs.text:
❌ No.

A class is loaded once per ClassLoader.

docs.title: Does loading execute the constructor?
docs.text:
❌ No.

Loading creates class metadata.

Constructors execute when objects are instantiated.

docs.title: Can one class be loaded multiple times?
docs.text:
✅ Yes.

If different ClassLoaders load the same class, each loaded version is treated as a distinct class by the JVM.

docs.title: Is Bootstrap ClassLoader written in Java?
docs.text:
❌ No.

It is implemented by the JVM.

docs.title: Does Class.forName() create an object?
docs.text:
❌ No.

It loads and initializes the class.

Object creation requires reflection (for example, calling a constructor) or the new operator.

docs.title: 20. Production Debugging Story
docs.text:
Problem

Spring Boot application failed during startup.

Error

NoClassDefFoundError:

org/postgresql/Driver

Investigation

  • Code compiled successfully.
  • The PostgreSQL JDBC driver JAR was missing from the runtime deployment.

Fix

Include the required dependency in the runtime package and verify the deployment artifact.

docs.text:
Interviewer:

"Your application throws NoClassDefFoundError after deployment, but it compiled successfully. What would you check?"

docs.title: Strong Answer
docs.text: I'd verify that the required dependency is present in the runtime classpath because NoClassDefFoundError often indicates a deployment issue rather than a compilation issue. I'd also check whether the class failed during static initialization, as that can produce the same error on subsequent access. Finally, I'd inspect the packaged JAR/WAR and application startup logs.

docs.title: 🎯 Interview Secret
docs.text:
When the interviewer asks:

"Why does Java use the Parent Delegation Model?"

Don't simply answer:

"Because that's how ClassLoaders work."

A senior-level answer is:

"Parent Delegation prevents core Java classes from being replaced by application classes, improving security and consistency. It also avoids loading the same class multiple times within a ClassLoader hierarchy, reducing duplication and ensuring that shared classes like java.lang.String have a single trusted definition."

This demonstrates an understanding of both JVM internals and the design rationale behind the ClassLoader architecture.

Chapter 34: Reflection API (Deep Dive)
docs.text:
Interview Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Frequently Asked In: Amazon, Oracle, Microsoft, Goldman Sachs, VMware, Spring Framework, Hibernate Interviews

docs.title: 1. Why Do Interviewers Ask This?
docs.text:
Reflection powers almost every major Java framework.

Examples:

  • Spring Boot
  • Spring DI
  • Spring MVC
  • Hibernate
  • Jackson
  • JUnit
  • Mockito
  • Lombok (partially, alongside annotation processing)
  • Dependency Injection frameworks

If you've worked with Spring, you've indirectly used Reflection thousands of times.

Typical interview questions:

  • What is Reflection?
  • Why is Reflection slower?
  • How does Spring create beans?
  • Can Reflection access private fields?
  • What are Method Handles?

docs.title: 2. 30-Second Interview Answer
docs.text: Reflection is a Java API that allows programs to inspect and manipulate classes, methods, fields, constructors, and annotations at runtime without knowing their details at compile time. Frameworks such as Spring, Hibernate, and Jackson rely heavily on Reflection for dependency injection, object creation, serialization, and annotation processing. Reflection is flexible but generally slower than direct method invocation because many compile-time optimisations cannot be applied.

docs.title: 3. What is Reflection?
docs.text:
Normally we write

Employee employee = new Employee();

employee.calculateSalary();

Compiler already knows

  • Class
  • Method
  • Fields

Everything is fixed.

Reflection allows us to discover them at runtime.

docs.title: 4. Reflection Architecture
docs.text:
Employee.class

                │

                ▼

        Reflection API

        ├──────────────┐
        ▼              ▼

    Fields          Methods

        ▼              ▼

   Constructors   Annotations

docs.title: 5. Getting a Class Object
docs.text: Three common approaches.

docs.title: Using .class
docs.text: Class<Employee> clazz = Employee.class;

docs.title: Using an Object
docs.text:
Employee employee = new Employee();

Class<?> clazz = employee.getClass();

docs.title: Using Class Name
docs.text:
Class<?> clazz =
    Class.forName("com.example.Employee");

Useful when the class name is only known at runtime.

docs.title: 6. Reading Class Information
docs.text:
Example

Class<?> clazz = Employee.class;

System.out.println(clazz.getName());

System.out.println(clazz.getSimpleName());

System.out.println(clazz.getPackageName());

Output

com.example.Employee

Employee

com.example

docs.title: 7. Accessing Fields
docs.text:
Example

public class Employee {

    private String name;

}

Reflection

Field field =
    Employee.class.getDeclaredField("name");

System.out.println(field.getName());

docs.title: 8. Reading Private Fields
docs.text:
Example

Employee employee =
    new Employee();

Reflection

Field field =
    Employee.class.getDeclaredField("name");

field.setAccessible(true);

System.out.println(field.get(employee));

Private fields can be accessed.

This is why Reflection should be used carefully.

docs.title: 9. Updating Private Fields
docs.text:
field.set(employee, "John");

Now

employee.getName();

returns

John

docs.title: 10. Calling Methods Dynamically
docs.text:
Example

Method method =
    Employee.class.getMethod("calculateSalary");

method.invoke(employee);

The method name is resolved at runtime.

docs.title: 11. Calling Private Methods
docs.text:
Example

Method method =
    Employee.class.getDeclaredMethod("calculate");

method.setAccessible(true);

method.invoke(employee);

Again,

Reflection bypasses normal access checks (subject to Java's module system and security restrictions in modern JDKs).

docs.title: 12. Constructors
docs.text:
Reflection can create objects.

Constructor<Employee> constructor =
    Employee.class.getConstructor();

Employee employee =
    constructor.newInstance();

This is how many frameworks instantiate classes.

docs.title: 13. Reading Annotations
docs.text:
Suppose

@Service
public class EmployeeService {

}

Reflection

Class<?> clazz =
    EmployeeService.class;

boolean present =
    clazz.isAnnotationPresent(Service.class);

Spring heavily relies on this.

docs.title: 14. Listing Methods
docs.text:
Method[] methods =
    Employee.class.getDeclaredMethods();

Frameworks inspect methods this way.

Example

save()

delete()

findById()

calculateSalary()

docs.title: 15. Reflection Performance
docs.text:
Interview favourite.

Direct call

employee.calculateSalary();

Reflection

method.invoke(employee);

Reflection is slower because:

  • Method lookup and invocation happen at runtime.
  • The JVM has fewer optimisation opportunities than with direct calls.
  • Access checks and additional indirection add overhead.

For most framework startup or configuration tasks, this overhead is acceptable.

docs.title: 16. Method Handles
docs.text:
Modern alternative.

Package

java.lang.invoke

Example

MethodHandles.Lookup lookup =
    MethodHandles.lookup();

Advantages

  • Better performance than traditional Reflection in many scenarios.
  • Designed to cooperate more closely with JVM optimisations.
  • Widely used in modern frameworks and language features.

Suppose

}

Jackson

↓

↓

Creates Object

↓

Reflection enables automatic JSON serialization and deserialization.

docs.title: Does Reflection break encapsulation?
docs.text:
✅ Yes.

It can access private members when permitted.

docs.title: Is Reflection always slow?
docs.text:
❌ No.

It is slower than direct invocation, but for many framework operations the overhead is insignificant because those operations are not on performance-critical paths.

docs.title: Does Spring use Reflection?
docs.text:
✅ Yes.

Spring uses Reflection extensively for bean creation, dependency injection, annotation scanning, and method invocation.

docs.title: Is Reflection compile-time or runtime?
docs.text: ✅ Runtime.

docs.title: Can Reflection create objects?
docs.text:
✅ Yes.

Using constructors discovered at runtime.

docs.text:
Spring Boot Startup

@Component

↓

Reflection

↓

Constructor Found

Object Created

↓

Dependency Injected

Without Reflection,

Spring would require manual wiring of every bean.

docs.title: 22. Production Debugging Story
docs.text:
Problem

A Spring Boot application failed during startup.

Error

NoSuchMethodException

Investigation

A framework attempted to instantiate an entity using Reflection.

The entity no longer had a no-argument constructor.

Root Cause

Hibernate could not create the object reflectively.

Fix

Add a suitable constructor (or configure the framework appropriately for the chosen constructor strategy).

docs.title: 24. Real Interview Scenario
docs.text:
Interviewer:

"Spring creates beans without you explicitly calling constructors. How?"

docs.title: Strong Answer
docs.text: During startup, Spring scans the classpath for annotated classes such as @Component, @Service, and @Repository. Using Reflection, it inspects constructors, creates object instances, resolves dependencies, and injects them into the appropriate fields or constructors. Reflection allows Spring to perform this dynamically without compile-time knowledge of the application's classes.

docs.title: 🎯 Interview Secret
docs.text:
When an interviewer asks:

"Why does Spring use Reflection?"

Don't answer:

"To call methods dynamically."

A senior-level answer is:

"Reflection enables Spring to discover application classes at runtime, inspect annotations, instantiate beans, inject dependencies, and invoke lifecycle methods without compile-time knowledge of the application's structure. This flexibility is what allows Spring's dependency injection and auto-configuration features to work."

This demonstrates that you understand not only the Reflection API but also how enterprise frameworks are built.

docs.title: Part VII – Class Loading, Reflection & Dynamic Proxies
Chapter 35: Dynamic Proxies (JDK Proxy, CGLIB & Spring AOP Internals)
docs.text:
Interview Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Frequently Asked In: Amazon, Oracle, Microsoft, Goldman Sachs, VMware, Spring Framework, Banking Product Companies

docs.title: 1. Why Do Interviewers Ask This?
docs.text:
Almost every Spring Boot application uses Dynamic Proxies.

Examples:

  • @Transactional
  • @Cacheable
  • @Async
  • @Retryable
  • @Validated
  • Spring Security
  • Logging AOP

Most developers use these annotations daily without understanding what happens internally.

Typical interview questions:

  • What is a Dynamic Proxy?
  • Why does Spring create proxies?
  • JDK Proxy vs CGLIB?
  • Why doesn't @Transactional work sometimes?
  • What is self-invocation?

docs.title: 2. 30-Second Interview Answer
docs.text: A Dynamic Proxy is an object generated at runtime that wraps another object and intercepts method calls. Spring uses proxies to implement Aspect-Oriented Programming (AOP), enabling features such as transactions, caching, logging, and security without modifying business logic. Spring uses JDK Dynamic Proxies for interface-based beans and CGLIB proxies for class-based beans.

docs.title: 3. Why Do We Need Proxies?
docs.text:
Suppose we have

public class PaymentService {

    public void transfer() {

        // Business Logic

    }

}

Now we need

  • Logging
  • Security
  • Transactions
  • Monitoring
  • Audit

Without proxies

public void transfer() {

    startTransaction();

    log();

    authenticate();

    // Business Logic

    commit();

}

Business code becomes cluttered.

docs.title: 4. Solution
docs.text:
Separate

Business Logic

from

Cross-Cutting Concerns

Using

Proxy

docs.title: 5. Proxy Architecture
docs.text:
Client

             │

             ▼

        Proxy Object

             │

     Before Advice

             │

             ▼

      Real Object

             │

      After Advice

The client talks to the proxy instead of the real object.

docs.title: 6. Static Proxy
docs.text:
Manually written.

Example

class PaymentProxy
        implements PaymentService {

    private PaymentService target;

    public void transfer() {

        log();

        target.transfer();

    }

}

Problems

  • Too much boilerplate
  • Difficult to maintain
  • Doesn't scale

docs.title: 7. Dynamic Proxy
docs.text:
Generated automatically at runtime.

No handwritten proxy class required.

JVM generates the proxy.

docs.title: 8. JDK Dynamic Proxy
docs.text:
Works

Only

for

Interfaces.

Example

public interface PaymentService {

    void transfer();

}

Implementation

public class PaymentServiceImpl
        implements PaymentService {

}

Spring creates

PaymentService Proxy

↓

PaymentServiceImpl

docs.title: 9. JDK Proxy Flow
docs.text:
Client

↓

Proxy

↓

InvocationHandler

↓

Real Object

Every method call passes through the InvocationHandler.

docs.title: 10. InvocationHandler
docs.text:
Core interface.

public Object invoke(

    Object proxy,

    Method method,

    Object[] args

)

This method intercepts every invocation.

docs.title: 11. Example
docs.text:
public Object invoke(...) {

    System.out.println("Before");

    Object result =
        method.invoke(target,args);

    System.out.println("After");

    return result;

}

This is the foundation of many AOP frameworks.

docs.title: 12. Limitation of JDK Proxy
docs.text:
Interview Favourite.

Suppose

public class PaymentService {

}

No interface.

JDK Proxy

❌ Cannot create a proxy.

Need

CGLIB

docs.title: 13. CGLIB
docs.text:
CGLIB creates a subclass at runtime.

Example

PaymentService

↓

Generated Subclass

↓

Intercept Methods

Unlike JDK proxies,

it doesn't require interfaces.

docs.title: 14. CGLIB Architecture
docs.text:
Client

↓

Generated Subclass

↓

Original Class

Method interception happens in the generated subclass.

docs.title: 15. Limitations of CGLIB
docs.text:
Cannot proxy

final class PaymentService

because

Final Class

↓

Cannot Extend

Similarly,

final void transfer()

cannot be overridden,

so it cannot be intercepted.

docs.title: 16. Spring Proxy Selection
docs.text:
Interview Favourite.

If bean implements

Interface

↓

Use

JDK Dynamic Proxy

Otherwise

↓

Use

CGLIB

Note: Modern Spring versions can also be configured to use CGLIB even when interfaces exist (for example, with proxyTargetClass=true).

docs.title: 17. Spring AOP Flow
docs.text:
Suppose

@Transactional

public void transfer()

Execution

Client

↓

Spring Proxy

↓

Begin Transaction

↓

Business Method

↓

Commit

↓

Return

The business method never manages the transaction directly.

docs.title: 18. How @Transactional Works
docs.text:
Internally

Method Called

↓

Proxy Intercepts

↓

Open Transaction

↓

Execute Method

↓

Commit

↓

Rollback (If Needed)

Exactly the same idea applies to:

  • @Cacheable
  • @Async
  • @Retryable

docs.title: 19. Self-Invocation Problem
docs.text:
One of the most common Spring interview questions.

Example

@Service

class PaymentService {

    public void methodA() {

        methodB();

    }

    @Transactional

    public void methodB() {

    }

}

Question

Will transaction start?

Answer

❌ No.

docs.title: 20. Why?
docs.text:
Because

methodA()

↓

Direct Call

↓

methodB()

The call never goes through

Spring Proxy

No interception.

No transaction.

docs.title: 21. Correct Flow
docs.text:
Client

↓

Proxy

↓

methodB()

Proxy intercepts.

Transaction starts.

docs.title: 22. Common Solutions
docs.text:
• Move the transactional method to another Spring bean.
  • Call through the Spring proxy instead of this.
  • Use AspectJ weaving when proxy-based AOP is insufficient.

The first option is usually the cleanest.

docs.title: 23. Performance
docs.text:
Interview Question

Are proxies slow?

Generally,

No.

The overhead is small compared to:

  • Database calls
  • HTTP requests
  • Disk I/O

Avoid using proxy-based interception inside extremely performance-sensitive tight loops.

docs.title: 24. Byte Buddy
docs.text:
Modern runtime code generation library.

Used by

  • Mockito
  • Hibernate (in some scenarios)
  • Various Java agents
  • Instrumentation frameworks

Advantages

  • Modern API
  • Flexible bytecode generation
  • Easier than ASM for many use cases

docs.title: 25. JDK Proxy vs CGLIB
docs.text: Feature JDK Proxy CGLIB Requires Interface ✅ Yes ❌ No Works with Classes ❌ No ✅ Yes Creates Proxy implementing interfaces Runtime subclass Can Proxy Final Class ❌ No ❌ No Can Proxy Final Method ❌ No ❌ No

docs.text:

↓

docs.text:
Problem

Developer reports:

@Transactional

Not Working

Investigation

Code

methodA()

↓

methodB()

Both methods

inside

same class.

Root Cause

Self-invocation bypassed the Spring proxy.

Fix

Move methodB() to another Spring-managed bean so that the call goes through the proxy.

docs.title: Does Spring modify your original class?
docs.text:
❌ No.

Spring creates a proxy around it.

docs.title: Is every Spring bean proxied?
docs.text:
❌ No.

Only beans requiring proxy-based features (AOP, transactions, caching, async, security, etc.) are proxied.

docs.title: Does JDK Proxy require interfaces?
docs.text: ✅ Yes.

docs.title: Can CGLIB proxy a final class?
Why does self-invocation fail?
docs.text: Because the call bypasses the proxy.

docs.title: 30. Real Interview Scenario
docs.text:
Interviewer:

"A method annotated with @Transactional isn't starting a transaction. What would you check?"

docs.title: Strong Answer
docs.text: First, I'd verify that the bean is managed by Spring and that transaction management is enabled. Then I'd check whether the method is being called through the Spring proxy. A common issue is self-invocation, where one method in a class directly calls another @Transactional method using this, bypassing the proxy. I'd also verify the method's visibility, transaction configuration, and logs to ensure the proxy is actually being created.

docs.title: 🎯 Interview Secret
docs.text:
When the interviewer asks:

"How does @Transactional work internally?"

Don't simply answer:

"Spring starts a transaction."

A senior-level answer is:

"Spring creates a proxy around the bean. When a client invokes a @Transactional method through that proxy, the proxy delegates to a transaction interceptor, which starts a transaction before invoking the target method. Depending on the outcome, it commits or rolls back the transaction. Because this mechanism is proxy-based by default, internal self-invocation bypasses the proxy and prevents transaction interception."

That answer demonstrates a solid understanding of Spring AOP, proxy internals, and transaction management, which is exactly what senior Java backend interviewers expect.

docs.title: 1. Why Do Interviewers Ask This?
docs.text:
Modern Java development revolves around annotations.

Almost everything in Spring Boot is annotation-driven:

  • @SpringBootApplication
  • @Component
  • @Service
  • @Repository
  • @Controller
  • @Transactional
  • @Autowired
  • @Configuration

Interviewers want to know:

  • How does Lombok work?
  • What is MapStruct?
  • Runtime vs compile-time annotations?

Typical interview question:

How does Spring discover and process annotations like @Service or @Autowired?

docs.title: 2. 30-Second Interview Answer
docs.text: Java annotations provide metadata about classes, methods, fields, and parameters. By themselves, annotations do nothing—they require a framework or tool to interpret them. Spring processes annotations at runtime using reflection and classpath scanning, while tools like Lombok and MapStruct process annotations at compile time using the Annotation Processing Tool (APT) to generate source code.

docs.title: 3. What Are Annotations?
docs.text:
Annotations provide

Metadata

They describe code rather than changing Java language behaviour by themselves.

Example

@Service
public class PaymentService {

}

@Service

does not execute any code on its own.

Spring interprets it.

docs.title: 4. Why Were Annotations Introduced?
docs.text:
Before annotations

Configuration was often written in XML.

Example

<bean id="paymentService"
      class="com.example.PaymentService"/>

Modern Spring

@Service
public class PaymentService {

}

Cleaner.

Less configuration.

docs.title: 5. Where Can Annotations Be Used?
docs.text:
Annotations can be applied to:

  • Classes
  • Methods
  • Fields
  • Constructors
  • Parameters
  • Packages
  • Local variables
  • Type uses (Java 8+)

Example

class Employee {

    @NotNull
    private String name;

}

docs.title: 6. Built-in Java Annotations
docs.text:
Common examples

Annotation Purpose @Override Verify overridden methods @Deprecated Mark deprecated APIs @SuppressWarnings Suppress compiler warnings @FunctionalInterface Ensure a single abstract method

docs.title: 7. Custom Annotation
docs.text:
Example

@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Target(ElementType.METHOD)
public @interface Audit {

}

Usage

@Audit
public void transfer() {

}

The annotation itself performs no action until code processes it.

docs.title: 8. Meta-Annotations
docs.text:
Meta-annotations define the behaviour of other annotations.

Most important ones:

  • @Target
  • @Retention
  • @Inherited
  • @Documented
  • @Repeatable

docs.title: 9. @Target
docs.text:
Specifies where an annotation can be used.

Example

@Target(ElementType.METHOD)

Only methods may be annotated.

Other common targets:

  • TYPE
  • FIELD
  • PARAMETER
  • CONSTRUCTOR

docs.title: 10. @Retention
docs.text:
Interview favourite.

Controls how long the annotation is retained.

Three options.

docs.title: SOURCE
docs.text:
Compiler

↓

Annotation Removed

Example

@Override

The compiler uses it, but it is not available at runtime.

docs.title: CLASS
docs.text:
Stored in the .class file but not retained for runtime reflection.

Used by some tools and bytecode processors.

docs.title: RUNTIME
docs.text:
Available through reflection.

Required by Spring.

Example

@Service

@Transactional

@Autowired

docs.title: 11. @Inherited
docs.text:
If applied to a class annotation,

subclasses inherit it.

Example

Parent

↓

Child

Only applies to class-level annotations.

docs.title: 12. @Documented
docs.text: Indicates the annotation should appear in generated Javadoc.

docs.title: 13. @Repeatable
docs.text:
Allows multiple instances of the same annotation.

Example

@Role("ADMIN")
@Role("AUDITOR")

docs.text:
Spring startup

Scan Classes

↓

Reflection

↓

Read Annotations

↓

Create Beans

↓

Dependency Injection

This happens every time the application starts.

Class<?> clazz =
    PaymentService.class;

boolean exists =
    clazz.isAnnotationPresent(Service.class);

Spring performs similar operations internally.

Interview favourite.

processing occurs

during compilation.

Chapter 37: Custom ClassLoaders, Plugin Architectures & ClassLoader Leaks
docs.text:
Interview Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Frequently Asked In: Amazon, Oracle, VMware, Red Hat, Atlassian, Spring, Tomcat, JVM Performance Interviews

docs.title: 1. Why Do Interviewers Ask This?
docs.text:
ClassLoaders are one of the least understood parts of the JVM.

However, they're heavily used by:

  • Spring Boot
  • Tomcat
  • IntelliJ IDEA
  • Maven
  • Jenkins
  • Kafka Connect
  • Plugin frameworks
  • OSGi

Understanding ClassLoaders helps explain:

  • Hot deployment
  • Plugin architectures
  • Metaspace leaks
  • Multiple versions of the same library
  • Application server internals

Typical interview questions:

  • What is a Custom ClassLoader?
  • Why do plugin systems use ClassLoaders?
  • What is a ClassLoader leak?
  • How does Tomcat isolate applications?
  • Can two versions of the same class exist?

docs.title: 2. 30-Second Interview Answer
docs.text: A ClassLoader is responsible for loading Java classes into the JVM. While the JVM provides Bootstrap, Platform, and Application ClassLoaders, applications can create Custom ClassLoaders to load classes from different sources such as plugins, remote locations, or encrypted JARs. Each ClassLoader creates its own namespace, allowing multiple versions of the same class to coexist. Improper management of ClassLoaders can lead to Metaspace memory leaks.

docs.title: 3. Why Do We Need Custom ClassLoaders?
docs.text:
Normally

Application

↓

Application ClassLoader

↓

Application Classes

But suppose

Users can install

Plugins

at runtime.

The Application ClassLoader cannot automatically load new JARs added after startup.

Need

Custom ClassLoader

docs.title: 4. Plugin Architecture
docs.text:
Main Application

        │

        ▼

Plugin Manager

        │

 ┌──────┴────────┐

 ▼               ▼

Plugin A     Plugin B

ClassLoader  ClassLoader

Each plugin has its own ClassLoader.

docs.text:
Suppose

Plugin A

uses

Jackson 2.15

Plugin B

uses

Jackson 2.18

Normally

↓

Conflict.

↓

No conflict.

Each plugin loads its own version.

docs.title: 6. Class Namespace
docs.text:
Interview favourite.

The JVM identifies a class by:

(ClassLoader, Fully Qualified Class Name)

Not simply

com.example.Employee

Therefore

Plugin1

↓

Employee.class

and

Plugin2

↓

Employee.class

are considered different classes if loaded by different ClassLoaders.

docs.title: 7. Custom ClassLoader Example
docs.text:
Simplified example

public class PluginClassLoader
        extends ClassLoader {

    @Override
    protected Class<?> findClass(String name)
            throws ClassNotFoundException {

        // Read class bytes

        return defineClass(
                name,
                bytes,
                0,
                bytes.length);

    }

}

Most custom loaders override findClass() while allowing the normal delegation process to remain intact.

docs.text:
One of the most important interview topics.

Suppose

Old ClassLoader

Metaspace

docs.title: 17. Common Causes of ClassLoader Leaks
docs.text:
• Static collections
  • ThreadLocal values not removed
  • Threads that continue running after undeploy
  • JDBC drivers not deregistered
  • Logging framework references
  • Caches holding application classes

docs.title: 19. Production Debugging Story
docs.text:
Problem

Tomcat server

↓

Applications redeployed daily

↓

Memory usage increased every day

Eventually

OutOfMemoryError:

Metaspace

Investigation

Heap dump

↓

MAT

↓

Reference chain

↓

Background scheduler thread

↓

Old WebApp ClassLoader

Root Cause

Thread never stopped during application shutdown.

Fix

  • Properly shut down executors.
  • Deregister resources.
  • Release ThreadLocal values.
  • Ensure application shutdown hooks clean up resources.

docs.title: 20. OSGi (High-Level)
docs.text:
OSGi is a module system where:

  • Each bundle has its own ClassLoader.
  • Bundles can be installed or removed dynamically.
  • Different bundle versions can coexist.
  • Services are shared through defined interfaces.

You don't need deep OSGi knowledge for most interviews, but knowing why it exists is useful.

docs.title: Can the same class exist twice?
docs.text:
✅ Yes.

If loaded by different ClassLoaders.

docs.title: Can two versions of the same library coexist?
docs.text:
✅ Yes.

With separate ClassLoaders.

docs.title: Is ClassLoader memory stored in the Heap?
docs.text:
❌ Not primarily.

Class metadata resides in Metaspace, while ClassLoader objects themselves are ordinary Java objects stored on the heap.

docs.title: Can GC unload classes?
docs.text:
✅ Yes.

But only when the associated ClassLoader is no longer reachable.

docs.title: Does undeploying a WAR automatically free Metaspace?
docs.text:
❌ Not always.

Only if all references to the application's ClassLoader have been released.

docs.title: 23. Real Interview Scenario
docs.text:
Interviewer:

"A Tomcat server runs fine initially, but after several application redeployments it throws OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace. What would you investigate?"

docs.title: Strong Answer
docs.text: I'd suspect a ClassLoader leak. I'd verify whether application threads, ThreadLocal values, static caches, JDBC drivers, or logging frameworks are retaining references to the old Web Application ClassLoader after undeployment. I'd analyse a heap dump with Eclipse MAT, inspect the reference chain to the ClassLoader, and ensure all application resources are properly cleaned up during shutdown.

docs.title: 🎯 Interview Secret
docs.text:
When the interviewer asks:

"Why does Tomcat use a separate ClassLoader for each web application?"

Don't simply answer:

"To load the application."

A senior-level answer is:

"Each web application gets its own ClassLoader to isolate dependencies and allow multiple applications with different library versions to run in the same Tomcat instance. It also enables independent deployment and undeployment. However, this design requires careful resource cleanup because lingering references can prevent the ClassLoader from being garbage collected, leading to Metaspace leaks."

That answer demonstrates an understanding of JVM internals, application server architecture, and real production troubleshooting.

Chapter 38: Spring IoC Container & Dependency Injection Internals
docs.text:
Interview Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Frequently Asked In: Amazon, Microsoft, Oracle, VMware, Goldman Sachs, JP Morgan, Morgan Stanley, Product Companies

docs.title: 1. Why Do Interviewers Ask This?
docs.text:
Every Spring Boot application depends on the IoC (Inversion of Control) Container.

When you write:

@Service
public class PaymentService {

}

or

@Autowired
private OrderRepository repository;

many developers simply assume "Spring does the magic."

Senior engineers understand what actually happens inside the Spring Container.

Typical interview questions:

  • What is IoC?
  • What is Dependency Injection?
  • How does Spring create beans?
  • What is BeanFactory?
  • What is ApplicationContext?
  • What happens during Spring Boot startup?

docs.title: 2. 30-Second Interview Answer
docs.text: Spring's IoC Container is responsible for creating, configuring, wiring, and managing application objects known as beans. During application startup, Spring scans the classpath, creates bean definitions, instantiates beans, injects dependencies, applies BeanPostProcessors, and stores beans in the ApplicationContext. Dependency Injection is simply the mechanism by which the container provides required dependencies instead of objects creating them manually.

docs.title: 3. What is Inversion of Control (IoC)?
docs.text:
Without IoC

public class PaymentService {

    private OrderRepository repository =
            new OrderRepository();

}

Problems:

  • Tight coupling
  • Difficult to test
  • Hard to replace implementations

With IoC

@Service
public class PaymentService {

    @Autowired
    private OrderRepository repository;

}

Now

Spring creates

↓

Spring injects

↓

Application uses

Control has been inverted from the application code to the container.

docs.text:

↓

↓

↓

↓

docs.title: 5. What is Dependency Injection (DI)?
docs.text:
Dependency Injection is one implementation of IoC.

Instead of

PaymentService

↓

↓

It becomes

↓

docs.title: 6. Types of Dependency Injection
docs.text: Spring supports

docs.title: Constructor Injection
docs.text:
✅ Recommended

@Service
public class PaymentService {

    private final OrderRepository repository;

    public PaymentService(
            OrderRepository repository) {

        this.repository = repository;
    }

}

docs.title: Setter Injection
docs.text:
@Autowired
public void setRepository(
        OrderRepository repository) {

    this.repository = repository;
}

Useful for optional dependencies.

docs.title: Field Injection
docs.text:
@Autowired
private OrderRepository repository;

Easy to write, but generally discouraged for new code because it makes testing and immutability harder.

docs.title: 7. Why Constructor Injection?
docs.text:
Interview Favourite.

Advantages:

  • Mandatory dependencies
  • Immutable fields
  • Easier unit testing
  • Detects circular dependencies earlier
  • Preferred by Spring documentation

docs.title: 8. BeanFactory
docs.text:
The most basic Spring container.

Responsibilities:

  • Create beans
  • Manage bean lifecycle
  • Dependency injection

Minimal features.

Rarely used directly in Spring Boot applications.

docs.title: 9. ApplicationContext
docs.text:
Most commonly used Spring container.

Extends BeanFactory.

Additional features:

  • Internationalization (i18n)
  • Event publishing
  • Resource loading
  • Environment abstraction
  • Bean post-processing
  • AOP integration

Almost every Spring Boot application uses an ApplicationContext.

docs.title: Is IoC the same as Dependency Injection?
docs.text:
❌ No.

IoC is the design principle.

DI is one technique used to implement IoC.

docs.title: Does Spring create every bean immediately?
docs.text:
❌ Not every bean.

By default, singleton beans are eagerly initialized, while lazy beans and some scoped beans are created later.

docs.title: Is BeanFactory obsolete?
docs.text:
❌ No.

ApplicationContext builds upon BeanFactory; the latter remains the core abstraction.

docs.title: Is field injection recommended?
docs.text:
❌ Generally no.

Constructor injection is preferred for mandatory dependencies.

docs.title: Can Spring have multiple ApplicationContexts?
docs.text:
✅ Yes.

For example, parent-child contexts or multiple deployed applications.

docs.title: 🎯 Interview Secret
docs.text:
When the interviewer asks:

"What does the Spring IoC Container actually do?"

Don't simply answer:

"It manages beans."

A senior-level answer is:

"The IoC container is responsible for the complete lifecycle of application objects. It discovers candidate classes, creates bean definitions, instantiates objects, resolves constructor and field dependencies, applies BeanPostProcessors and AOP proxies where required, manages bean scopes and lifecycle callbacks, and exposes fully initialized beans through the ApplicationContext. This centralised management enables loose coupling, easier testing, and consistent lifecycle management."

That answer demonstrates a deep understanding of Spring internals, not just annotation usage.

  • How @PostConstruct works
  • How @Transactional works
  • How AOP proxies are created
  • How custom framework extensions work

Typical interview questions:

  • Explain the Spring Bean Lifecycle.
  • What is a BeanPostProcessor?
  • Difference between BeanFactoryPostProcessor and BeanPostProcessor?
  • When is @PostConstruct executed?

docs.title: 2. 30-Second Interview Answer
docs.text: During startup, Spring creates bean definitions, instantiates bean objects, injects dependencies, invokes aware callbacks, executes BeanPostProcessors, runs initialization methods such as @PostConstruct or afterPropertiesSet(), and finally exposes the bean for use. Before application shutdown, Spring invokes destruction callbacks such as @PreDestroy and destroy(). BeanPostProcessors allow Spring to modify or wrap beans—for example, by creating AOP proxies for transactions and security.

Interviewer:

"At what stage does Spring create an AOP proxy?"

docs.title: Strong Answer
docs.text: Spring first creates and wires the target bean. During the post-processing phase, BeanPostProcessor implementations—such as Spring's auto-proxy creators—inspect the bean. If AOP advice such as @Transactional applies, they create and return a proxy instead of the original bean. The proxy is then stored in the ApplicationContext and injected into dependent beans.

docs.title: 🎯 Interview Secret
docs.text:
When the interviewer asks:

"What is the most important extension point in the Spring Bean Lifecycle?"

Don't simply answer:

"BeanPostProcessor."

A senior-level answer is:

"BeanPostProcessor is one of Spring's most powerful extension points because it allows the container to inspect, modify, or replace bean instances after creation but before they're exposed to the application. Spring uses this mechanism to implement AOP proxies, transaction management, caching, asynchronous execution, validation, and many other framework features without requiring changes to business code."

This answer demonstrates that you understand how Spring's infrastructure is built, not just how to use its annotations.

Chapter 40: Spring Boot Auto-Configuration & Starter Internals

Interview Difficulty: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Frequently Asked In: Amazon, Microsoft, Oracle, VMware, Goldman Sachs, JP Morgan, Product Companies

docs.title: 1. Why Do Interviewers Ask This?
docs.text:
One of Spring Boot's biggest advantages is that it eliminates large amounts of configuration.

You simply add a dependency like:

spring-boot-starter-web

Run the application...

...and suddenly you have:

  • Embedded Tomcat
  • DispatcherServlet
  • Jackson
  • REST support
  • Error handling
  • Validation
  • Logging

The obvious question is:

"How did Spring Boot know to configure all of this?"

Understanding Auto-Configuration separates developers who use Spring Boot from engineers who understand Spring Boot.

Typical interview questions:

  • What is Auto-Configuration?
  • How does @SpringBootApplication work?
  • What is @EnableAutoConfiguration?
  • What are conditional annotations?
  • What is a Spring Boot Starter?
  • How would you create your own starter?

docs.title: 2. 30-Second Interview Answer
docs.text: Spring Boot Auto-Configuration automatically configures application components based on the dependencies available on the classpath, existing beans, and application properties. During startup, @EnableAutoConfiguration imports auto-configuration classes that are conditionally applied using annotations such as @ConditionalOnClass and @ConditionalOnMissingBean. This allows Spring Boot to provide sensible defaults while still allowing developers to override them.

↓

docs.title: 21. Production Debugging Story
docs.text:
Problem

Developer expected

ObjectMapper

to be customised.

But application still used the default configuration.

Investigation

A custom bean was declared with a different name but not of the expected type.

Spring Boot therefore did not detect an existing ObjectMapper bean, so its own auto-configuration still executed.

Fix

Register the custom bean with the correct type so @ConditionalOnMissingBean(ObjectMapper.class) prevents the default bean from being created.

docs.title: Does Auto-Configuration always create every bean?
docs.text:
❌ No.

It creates beans only when conditions are satisfied.

docs.title: Can developers override Auto-Configuration?
docs.text:
✅ Yes.

Providing your own bean is often enough because many auto-configurations use @ConditionalOnMissingBean.

docs.title: Is a Starter the same as Auto-Configuration?
docs.text:
❌ No.

A Starter is a dependency.

Auto-Configuration is the Java configuration logic that the dependency enables.

docs.title: Does @ComponentScan perform Auto-Configuration?
docs.text:
❌ No.

It discovers your application's components.

Auto-Configuration is handled separately.

docs.title: Does Spring Boot force embedded Tomcat?
docs.text:
❌ No.

You can replace it with Jetty or Undertow by changing dependencies.

Those classes use conditions such as @ConditionalOnClass(DataSource.class) and @ConditionalOnMissingBean(DataSource.class) to determine whether configuration should be applied. If the required libraries are present, configuration properties are available, and the application hasn't already defined its own DataSource, Spring Boot creates and registers one automatically.

docs.title: 🎯 Interview Secret
docs.text:
When the interviewer asks:

"How does Spring Boot know which beans to create?"

Don't answer:

"It scans the classpath."

A senior-level answer is:

"Spring Boot imports a predefined set of auto-configuration classes through @EnableAutoConfiguration. Each auto-configuration class contains conditional logic that checks the classpath, configuration properties, and existing beans. Only when those conditions are satisfied are the corresponding beans registered. This conditional approach allows Spring Boot to provide sensible defaults while remaining highly customisable."

That answer demonstrates an understanding of Spring Boot internals, not just its convenience features.

docs.text:
Every HTTP request in a Spring MVC or Spring Boot application passes through the DispatcherServlet.

When a client sends:

docs.title: 2. 30-Second Interview Answer
docs.text: DispatcherServlet is the front controller of Spring MVC. Every HTTP request first reaches the DispatcherServlet, which delegates to HandlerMapping to locate the appropriate controller, uses a HandlerAdapter to invoke it, processes request and response bodies through HttpMessageConverters, handles exceptions when necessary, and finally returns the HTTP response to the client.

docs.title: Does DispatcherServlet call controllers directly?
docs.text:
❌ No.

It delegates through HandlerMapping and HandlerAdapter.

docs.title: Does @RequestBody use Reflection?
docs.text:
Indirectly, yes.

Spring uses Jackson, which relies on reflection (and other mechanisms) to create and populate Java objects.

docs.title: Does every request create a new DispatcherServlet?
docs.text:
❌ No.

Typically, one DispatcherServlet instance handles many requests concurrently.

docs.title: Does ViewResolver handle REST APIs?
docs.text:
❌ Generally no.

REST responses use HttpMessageConverter.

docs.text:
✅ Yes.

docs.text:
Interviewer:

"A REST endpoint is returning HTTP 415 (Unsupported Media Type). How would you investigate?"

docs.title: Strong Answer
docs.text: I'd first verify the request's Content-Type header and compare it with what the controller expects. If the endpoint uses @RequestBody, Spring requires an appropriate HttpMessageConverter for that media type. I'd also check whether Jackson is on the classpath, review any custom message converter configuration, and inspect the application logs to determine why the request couldn't be deserialized.

docs.title: 🎯 Interview Secret
docs.text:
When the interviewer asks:

"How does a Spring MVC request reach the controller?"

Don't answer:

"DispatcherServlet calls the controller."

A senior-level answer is:

"Every request first reaches the DispatcherServlet, which acts as the Front Controller. It consults a HandlerMapping to identify the appropriate controller method, delegates invocation to a HandlerAdapter, resolves method arguments such as @PathVariable and @RequestBody, executes the controller, and finally uses HttpMessageConverters to serialize the response. Exceptions are handled through HandlerExceptionResolvers before the response is sent back to the client."

That answer demonstrates a clear understanding of the complete Spring MVC request pipeline, rather than only the controller layer.

docs.text:
Nearly every enterprise application requires security.

docs.title: 2. 30-Second Interview Answer
docs.text: Spring Security secures applications using a chain of servlet filters. Every request passes through the Security Filter Chain before reaching Spring MVC. The framework authenticates the user, stores the authentication in the SecurityContext, performs authorization checks, and only then allows the request to reach the controller. Features such as JWT, OAuth2, method security, and session-based authentication all build on this architecture.

docs.title: Does Spring Security protect controllers directly?
docs.text:
❌ No.

It intercepts requests using servlet filters before controllers are invoked.

docs.title: Is JWT encrypted?
docs.text:
❌ Not necessarily.

A typical signed JWT (JWS) is signed, not encrypted. Its payload is Base64URL-encoded and can be read by anyone holding the token, so sensitive data should not be stored in it unless encryption (JWE) is specifically used.

docs.title: Strong Answer
docs.text: I'd first verify that the JWT filter is actually part of the Security Filter Chain and executes before authorization. Then I'd check whether the token signature, issuer, audience, and expiry are valid. I'd also confirm that the filter creates an authenticated Authentication object and stores it in the SecurityContext. Finally, I'd review the security configuration and logs to ensure the request matches the intended security rules.

docs.title: 🎯 Interview Secret
docs.text:
When the interviewer asks:

"How does Spring Security authenticate a JWT request?"

Don't answer:

"It validates the token."

A senior-level answer is:

"Every incoming request first passes through the Security Filter Chain. A JWT authentication filter extracts the Bearer token from the Authorization header, validates its signature and claims, and if valid, creates an authenticated Authentication object. That object is stored in the SecurityContext, allowing subsequent authorization filters and controller methods to determine the user's identity and permissions. Only after these checks does the request proceed to the DispatcherServlet."

That answer demonstrates an understanding of Spring Security's architecture, filter chain, authentication flow, and request lifecycle, rather than just JWT concepts.
